> - Finding the values of $2 x$ first and halving at the end is far safer than halving as you go
> 
> A negative tangent means the calculator value is outside almost any exam range.
> 
> - `\text{tan}^{- 1} \left(- 7\right)` gives $- 81 . 869 \circ$, which is not an answer, it is a starting point
> - Add $180 \circ$ until you are inside the range, then keep adding $180 \circ$ until you leave it
> 
> Keep the unrounded values of $2 x$ until the halving.
> 
> - Rounding $98 . 130 \circ$ to $98 \circ$ first gives $x = 49 \circ$, which happens to be right here, but the habit will cost marks elsewhere

parts.problemMd:
![Triangle AOB and sector BOC. OA is 10 cm, OB and OC are 6 cm each, and arc BC is π cm. Centred at O, labelled as Figure 1.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-further-maths-19/geometry-and-trigonometry/trigonometric-formulae-and-identities/assets/010-triangle-aob-and-sector-boc-oa-is-10-cm-ob-and-o.png)

Figure 1 shows a shape $ABC$in which $AOB$ is a triangle, $AOC$ is a straight line and $OBC$ is a sector of a circle with centre $O$.

$AO=10$cm $,OC=OB=6$cm and the length of arc $BC=π$ cm.

Find, to 3 significant figures, the length of $AB$.
parts.solutionMd:
$A B$ is a side of triangle $A O B$, and two of its sides are already known, so the angle between them is what is needed

The arc length formula $s = r θ$ links the arc, the radius and the angle at the centre, with the angle in radians

$π = 6 θ$

$θ = \frac{π}{6}$

$A O C$ is a straight line, so the angles at $O$ add up to $π$

`\angle A O B = \pi - \frac{\pi}{6}`

`\angle A O B = \frac{5 \pi}{6}`

**[B1]**

Triangle $A O B$ now has two sides and the angle between them, which is exactly what the cosine rule needs

`A B^{2} = 10^{2} + 6^{2} - 2 \times 10 \times 6 \times \text{cos} \left(\frac{5 \pi}{6}\right)`

**[M1]**

Since `\text{cos} \left(\frac{5 \pi}{6}\right)` is negative, subtracting it adds to the total

$A B^{2} = 136 + 60 \sqrt{3}$

$A B = 15 . 4894 \dots$

$A B = 15 . 5 \text{  cm  } \left(3 s . f .\right)$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Uses the arc length to find $θ = \frac{π}{6}$ and hence `\angle A O B = \frac{5 \pi}{6}`. Working in degrees is equally acceptable, so `\angle A O B = 150^{\circ}` earns this mark.
> 
> **M1**: A correct cosine rule statement using 10, 6 and your angle $A O B$.
> 
> **A1**: $15 . 5$ cm. Accept answers which round to this value.
> 
> The whole question may be worked in degrees throughout, provided the calculator is in the matching mode.
> 
> The angle at $O$ inside the triangle must be the obtuse one. Using $\frac{π}{6}$ in the cosine rule gives $5 . 71$ cm and earns the method mark only.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The arc length is there to give you an angle, not a length.
> 
> - $s = r θ$ rearranges to $θ = \frac{π}{6}$ in one step, and that angle is the sector's, not the triangle's
> - The formula only works when $θ$ is in radians
> 
> The straight line $A O C$ is the key fact in the diagram.
> 
> - It means the two angles at $O$ add to $π$, so subtracting $\frac{π}{6}$ leaves `\angle A O B = \frac{5 \pi}{6}`
> - Reaching for $\frac{π}{6}$ in the cosine rule is the single commonest error here, and the diagram makes it obvious that $A B$ is far longer than 6 cm
> 
> Two sides and the angle between them always means the cosine rule.
> 
> - The sine rule needs an angle opposite a known side, and there is not one here
> 
> A negative cosine makes the answer bigger, which is a useful check.
> 
> - `\text{cos} \left(\frac{5 \pi}{6}\right) = - \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}`, so the $- 2 a b \text{cos} C$ term turns into $+ 60 \sqrt{3}$
> - An answer smaller than 10 cm would mean the sign has gone wrong

parts.problemMd:
![Diagram of a pyramid with triangular base ABC and apex O. Sides OA and OC are 12 cm, AB and AC are 8 cm, and height OD is labelled. Diagram not to scale.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-further-maths-19/geometry-and-trigonometry/trigonometric-formulae-and-identities/assets/009-diagram-of-a-pyramid-with-triangular-base-abc-an.png)

Figure 2 shows a right pyramid $ABCDO$with a horizontal square base of side 8 cm. The vertical height of the pyramid is $h$ cm and $OA=OB=OC=OD=12$ cm.

Find the exact value of $h$.
parts.solutionMd:
In a right pyramid the apex sits directly above the centre of the base, so start by locating that centre

Let $M$ be the point where the diagonals of the square cross, so $O M$ is the vertical height $h$

The diagonal of the square is the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle with two sides of 8

$A C = \sqrt{8^{2}+8^{2}}$

$A C = 8 \sqrt{2}$

**[M1]**

$M$ is the midpoint of that diagonal, so $A M$ is half of it

$A M = 4 \sqrt{2}$

Triangle $O M A$ has a right angle at $M$, with $O A = 12$ as its hypotenuse

$h = \sqrt{12^{2}-(4\sqrt{2})^{2}}$

**[M1]**

$h = \sqrt{112}$

$112 = 16 \times 7$, so the surd simplifies

$h = 4 \sqrt{7}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: A correct method for the diagonal of the base, or for half of it, so $8 \sqrt{2}$ or $4 \sqrt{2}$.
> 
> **M1**: A correct use of Pythagoras in a right-angled triangle containing $h$, $O A$ and half the diagonal.
> 
> **A1**: $h = 4 \sqrt{7}$.
> 
> The question asks for the exact value, so $10 . 58$ does not earn the accuracy mark.
> 
> Working with the diagonal $B D$ instead of $A C$ is equally acceptable, since they are the same length and cross at the same point.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The first move in every pyramid question is to find the foot of the vertical height.
> 
> - For a right pyramid on a square base that is the centre of the square, where the diagonals cross
> - Sketching the single right-angled triangle $O M A$ separately, out of the three-dimensional picture, makes the rest straightforward
> 
> Half the diagonal is the length you need, not the side.
> 
> - The sloping edge $O A$ runs to a corner, so the horizontal distance is $A M$, not 4
> - Using 4 by mistake gives $h = \sqrt{128}$, which is the commonest wrong answer here
> 
> Keep the surds exact all the way through.
> 
> - $( 4 \sqrt{2} )^{2} = 32$ exactly, so $h^{2}$ is $144 - 32$, which is $112$ with no rounding at all
> - Simplify $\sqrt{112}$ by looking for the largest square factor, which is 16

parts.problemMd: Find, to 1 decimal place, the size of the angle between $OA$ and the plane $ABCD$.
parts.solutionMd:
The angle between a line and a plane is the angle between the line and its shadow on that plane

$O$ is directly above $M$, so the shadow of $O A$ on the base is $M A$, and the angle wanted is `\angle O A M`

That is the angle at $A$ in the same right-angled triangle used in part (a)

The height is opposite it and $A M$ is adjacent to it, so use the tangent

`\text{tan} \angle O A M = \frac{4 \sqrt{7}}{4 \sqrt{2}}`

**[M1]**

`\angle O A M = 61.8744 \ldots ^{\circ}`

`\angle O A M = 61.9 ^{\circ} \textrm{ } (1 d.p.)`

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: A correct trigonometric statement for the angle between $O A$ and the base, using your $h$ and half the diagonal.
> 
> **A1**: Accept answers which round to $61 . 9 ^{\circ}$.
> 
> Any equivalent trigonometry is acceptable, so `\text{cos} \angle O A M = \frac{4 \sqrt{2}}{12}` or `\text{sin} \angle O A M = \frac{4 \sqrt{7}}{12}` both earn the method mark.

> **[exam-tip]**
> A line meets a plane at the angle between the line and its shadow.
> 
> - Shine a light straight down: $O A$ casts the shadow $M A$, so the angle is at $A$ between $O A$ and $M A$
> - That phrasing turns every "line and plane" question into an ordinary right-angled triangle
> 
> You already have the triangle from part (a), so do not build a new one.
> 
> - $O M A$ has the right angle at $M$, height $4 \sqrt{7}$, base $4 \sqrt{2}$ and hypotenuse 12
> - All three sides are known, so any of sine, cosine or tangent will work
> 
> Use the exact values rather than the rounded ones.
> 
> - $\frac{4\sqrt{7}}{4\sqrt{2}}$ typed straight into the calculator avoids carrying $10 . 58$ through
> - On a 1 decimal place answer that rarely matters, but the habit protects you when it does

parts.problemMd: Find, to 1 decimal place, the size of the angle between the plane $AOB$ and the plane $ABCD$.
parts.solutionMd:
Two planes meet along a line, and the angle between them is measured in the direction perpendicular to that line

Plane $A O B$ and the base meet along $A B$, so work at the point of $A B$ closest to the centre

Let $N$ be the midpoint of $A B$. Then $O N$ is perpendicular to $A B$, and so is $M N$

So the angle between the planes is `\angle O N M`

$M N$ runs from the centre of the square to the middle of a side, which is half the side length

$M N = 4$

Triangle $O M N$ has its right angle at $M$, with the height opposite `\angle O N M`

`\text{tan} \angle O N M = \frac{4 \sqrt{7}}{4}`

**[M1]**

`\angle O N M = 69.2951 \ldots ^{\circ}`

`\angle O N M = 69.3 ^{\circ} \textrm{ } (1 d.p.)`

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: A correct trigonometric statement for the angle between the two planes, using your $h$ and a horizontal distance of 4.
> 
> **A1**: Accept answers which round to $69 . 3 ^{\circ}$.
> 
> Any equivalent trigonometry is acceptable. Working through the slant height $O N = \sqrt{128}$ and using `\text{cos} \angle O N M = \frac{4}{\sqrt{128}}` reaches the same angle.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The hard part of a plane-to-plane angle is choosing where to measure it.
> 
> - Find the line where the two planes meet, here $A B$, then move perpendicular to it in each plane
> - $O N$ and $M N$ are both perpendicular to $A B$, which is exactly what makes `\angle O N M` the right angle to find
> 
> The horizontal distance changes between parts (b) and (c), and the height does not.
> 
> - Part (b) runs to a corner, so the horizontal distance is $4 \sqrt{2}$
> - Part (c) runs to the middle of a side, so it is only 4, which is why this angle is the larger of the two
> 
> Check that your two answers are consistent.
> 
> - A shorter horizontal distance with the same height must give a steeper angle
> - $69 . 3 ^{\circ}$ being bigger than $61 . 9 ^{\circ}$ is a quick confirmation that neither has been mixed up

parts.problemMd:
The midpoint of $OA$is  $P$ and $Q$ is the point on $BC$ such that $BQ:QC=3:1$

Show that $PQ=4\sqrt{5}$ cm.
parts.solutionMd:
$P$ and $Q$ are at different heights, so split $P Q$ into a vertical part and a horizontal part

$P$ is the midpoint of $O A$, and $O$ is directly above the centre $M$

So $P$ sits directly above $S$, the midpoint of $A M$, at exactly half the height of the pyramid

$P S = \frac{4\sqrt{7}}{2}$

$P S = 2 \sqrt{7}$

**[M1]**

Everything else happens in the horizontal base, so set up coordinates there

Take $A$ as the origin, with $A B$ along one axis and $A D$ along the other

Then $A$ is $( 0 , 0 )$, $B$ is $( 8 , 0 )$, $C$ is $( 8 , 8 )$ and the centre $M$ is $( 4 , 4 )$

$S$ is the midpoint of $A M$, so $S$ is $( 2 , 2 )$

$B Q : Q C = 3 : 1$ and $B C = 8$, so $B Q = 6$ and $Q$ is $( 8 , 6 )$

$S Q^{2} = ( 8 - 2 )^{2} + ( 6 - 2 )^{2}$

$S Q^{2} = 52$

**[A1]**

$P S$ is vertical and $S Q$ is horizontal, so they are at right angles and Pythagoras applies

$P Q^{2} = ( 2 \sqrt{7} )^{2} + 52$

**[M1]**

$P Q^{2} = 80$

$P Q = 4 \sqrt{5}  \text{cm as required}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Finds the height of $P$ above the base as half of $h$, so $2 \sqrt{7}$.
> 
> **A1**: A correct horizontal distance from the point below $P$ to $Q$, so $S Q^{2} = 52$ or $S Q = \sqrt{52}$.
> 
> **M1**: Uses Pythagoras with a vertical and a horizontal distance to reach $P Q$.
> 
> **A1**: Reaches the given answer $4 \sqrt{5}$ with no errors.
> 
> The answer is given, so the working must be complete.
> 
> Any equivalent system of right-angled triangles is acceptable. Dropping a perpendicular from $P$ to the diagonal $A C$ and then a second perpendicular across to $B C$ reaches $P Q$ in two steps and earns the same marks.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Any distance in three dimensions splits into one vertical piece and one horizontal piece.
> 
> - Find the point directly below the higher end, then work out the horizontal distance from there
> - One application of Pythagoras then finishes it, no matter how awkward the two points look
> 
> Coordinates on the base are worth the thirty seconds they take.
> 
> - $S$ at $( 2 , 2 )$ and $Q$ at $( 8 , 6 )$ makes the horizontal distance a routine calculation
> - Trying to chase the distance round the square with separate triangles is where errors creep in
> 
> Halving works all the way down for a midpoint.
> 
> - $P$ is halfway along $O A$, so it is at half the height and half the horizontal distance from $A$
> - That is what puts $S$ at the midpoint of $A M$ rather than anywhere else
> 
> Read the ratio carefully.
> 
> - $B Q : Q C = 3 : 1$ means $Q$ is three quarters of the way from $B$ to $C$, so $B Q = 6$
> - Reading it the other way round gives $B Q = 2$ and the proof will not close

parts.problemMd: Find, to 1 decimal place, the size of angle $PQA$.
parts.solutionMd:
Triangle $P Q A$ has no right angle, so aim to find all three sides and then use the cosine rule

$A$ and $Q$ both lie in the base, so $A Q$ is a horizontal distance and the coordinates from part (d) give it directly

$A Q = \sqrt{8^{2}+6^{2}}$

$A Q = 10$

**[M1]**

$P$ is the midpoint of $O A$, and $O A = 12$

$P A = 6$

Part (d) gives the third side, $P Q = 4 \sqrt{5}$

The angle wanted is at $Q$, so $P A$ is the side opposite it

`\text{cos} \angle P Q A = \frac{10^{2} + (4 \sqrt{5})^{2} - 6^{2}}{2 \times 10 \times 4 \sqrt{5}}`

**[M1]**

`\text{cos} \angle P Q A = 0.80498 \ldots`

**[A1]**

`\angle P Q A = 36.39124 \ldots ^{\circ}`

`\angle P Q A = 36.4 ^{\circ} \textrm{ } (1 d.p.)`

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: A correct method for $A Q$, giving 10.
> 
> **M1**: A correct substitution into the cosine rule for the angle at $Q$, using your three side lengths.
> 
> **A1**: A correct value or expression for `\text{cos} \angle P Q A`.
> 
> **A1**: Accept answers which round to $36 . 4 ^{\circ}$.
> 
> Follow through from your own value of $P Q$ in part (d).
> 
> Splitting triangle $P Q A$ with a perpendicular and using right-angled trigonometry is equally acceptable, provided the final angle is the one at $Q$.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The two previous parts have already done most of the work.
> 
> - $P Q = 4 \sqrt{5}$ comes from part (d), and $P A = 6$ is half of the given $O A$
> - Only $A Q$ is new, and it is a flat distance in the base
> 
> Three sides and an angle to find is always the cosine rule.
> 
> - Rearranged, it is $\text{cos} C = \frac{a^{2}+b^{2}-c^{2}}{2ab}$
> - The side that goes on top as $c$ is the one opposite the angle you want, here $P A$
> 
> Getting the wrong angle is the easiest mark to lose here.
> 
> - `\angle P Q A` is at $Q$, so $P A$ is the opposite side
> - Putting $P Q$ on top instead gives the angle at $A$, which is a perfectly good angle but the wrong one
> 
> Squares of surds are exact, so nothing needs rounding until the end.
> 
> - $( 4 \sqrt{5} )^{2} = 80$ exactly, so the numerator is $100 + 80 - 36 = 144$
> - Only the final division and the inverse cosine need the calculator at all

parts.problemMd: Show that $\mathrm{cos}(A-B)--\mathrm{cos}(A+B)=2\mathrm{sin}A\mathrm{sin}B$
parts.solutionMd:
Both sides of this identity involve $A$ and $B$ separately on the right and combined on the left, so expand the two compound angles

Use the addition formulae for cosine, which differ only in the sign of the second term

$\text{cos} ( A - B ) = \text{cos} A \text{cos} B + \text{sin} A \text{sin} B$

$\text{cos} ( A + B ) = \text{cos} A \text{cos} B - \text{sin} A \text{sin} B$

**[M1]**

Subtract the second from the first, taking care with the signs inside the bracket

$\text{cos} ( A - B ) - \text{cos} ( A + B ) = \text{cos} A \text{cos} B + \text{sin} A \text{sin} B - \text{cos} A \text{cos} B + \text{sin} A \text{sin} B$

The two $\text{cos} A \text{cos} B$ terms cancel and the two $\text{sin} A \text{sin} B$ terms add

$\text{cos} ( A - B ) - \text{cos} ( A + B ) = 2 \text{sin} A \text{sin} B  \text{as required}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Expands both $\text{cos} ( A - B )$ and $\text{cos} ( A + B )$ correctly using the addition formulae.
> 
> **A1**: Subtracts them correctly and reaches the given result with no errors.
> 
> The result is given in the question, so every line has to be correct. Starting from the right-hand side and working back to the left is equally acceptable.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Both cosine addition formulae are on the formulae sheet, so quote them rather than trusting memory.
> 
> - The sign flips: $\text{cos} ( A + B )$ takes a minus and $\text{cos} ( A - B )$ takes a plus
> - That sign flip is the entire reason the subtraction leaves $2 \text{sin} A \text{sin} B$ behind
> 
> The bracket in the subtraction is where marks are lost.
> 
> - Subtracting $- \text{sin} A \text{sin} B$ gives $+ \text{sin} A \text{sin} B$, so the sine terms add rather than cancel
> - Write the second expansion inside brackets before you subtract, then remove them in a separate step
> 
> This identity is the product-to-sum result, and it is worth recognising.
> 
> - It turns a product of two sines into a difference of two cosines, which is exactly what makes part (c) integrable
> - A product of trigonometric functions cannot be integrated directly, so questions like this almost always convert first

parts.problemMd: Hence express $2\mathrm{sin}5x\mathrm{sin}3x$ in the form  $\mathrm{cos}mx-\mathrm{cos}nx$where $m$ and  $n$ are integers, giving the value of $m$ and the value of $n$,
parts.solutionMd:
The word "hence" means part (a) does the work, so match the two expressions up

Part (a) says $2 \text{sin} A \text{sin} B = \text{cos} ( A - B ) - \text{cos} ( A + B )$, and here the product is $2 \text{sin} 5 x \text{sin} 3 x$

So take $A = 5 x$ and $B = 3 x$

$A - B = 5 x - 3 x$

$A - B = 2 x$

$A + B = 5 x + 3 x$

$A + B = 8 x$

Substitute those two angles into the result from part (a)

$2 \text{sin} 5 x \text{sin} 3 x = \text{cos} 2 x - \text{cos} 8 x$

**[B1]**

so $m = 2$ and $n = 8$

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: $\text{cos} 2 x - \text{cos} 8 x$, with both values identified.
> 
> The terms must be in this order, since the form given in the question is $\text{cos} m x - \text{cos} n x$. Writing $\text{cos} 8 x - \text{cos} 2 x$ has the sign the wrong way round and earns nothing.

> **[exam-tip]**
> "Hence" is an instruction, not a suggestion.
> 
> - The one mark here is for spotting that $A = 5 x$ and $B = 3 x$ turns part (a) straight into the answer
> - Expanding from scratch wastes several minutes and risks a sign slip
> 
> Check which of $m$ and $n$ is which before you write the answer down.
> 
> - The difference $A - B$ goes with the plus sign in the identity, so $\text{cos} 2 x$ comes first
> - Getting them the wrong way round changes the sign of the whole expression

parts.problemMd:
(i) Find `integral 4 sin space 5 theta space sin 3 theta space straight d theta`

(ii) Hence evaluate $\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{6}} 4 sin  5 \theta  sin 3 \theta  d \theta$, giving your answer in the form  $\frac{a\sqrt{b}}{c}$ where $a$, $b$ and  $c$ are integers.
parts.solutionMd:
**(i)**

A product of two sines cannot be integrated as it stands, so use part (b) to turn it into a sum

Part (b) gives $2 \text{sin} 5 x \text{sin} 3 x = \text{cos} 2 x - \text{cos} 8 x$, and here the coefficient is 4 rather than 2

So the integrand is twice the expression from part (b), with $θ$ in place of $x$

`\int 4 \text{sin} 5 \theta \text{sin} 3 \theta \text{d} \theta = 2 \int \left(\text{cos} 2 \theta - \text{cos} 8 \theta\right) \text{d} \theta`

**[M1]**

Integrating $\text{cos} k θ$ gives $\frac{\text{sin}kθ}{k}$, so divide each term by the multiple of $θ$ inside it

`\int 4 \text{sin} 5 \theta \text{sin} 3 \theta \text{d} \theta = 2 \left[\frac{\text{sin} 2 \theta}{2} - \frac{\text{sin} 8 \theta}{8}\right] + c`

**[A1]**

**(ii)**

"Hence" again, so use the integral you have just found and put the limits in

`\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{6}} 4 \text{sin} 5 \theta \text{sin} 3 \theta \text{d} \theta = 2 \left[\frac{\text{sin} 2 \theta}{2} - \frac{\text{sin} 8 \theta}{8}\right]_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{6}}`

At the upper limit the two angles are $\frac{π}{3}$ and $\frac{4π}{3}$

$\text{sin} \frac{π}{3} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$

$\text{sin} \frac{4π}{3} = - \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$

At the lower limit both sines are zero, so that whole bracket contributes nothing

`\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{6}} 4 \text{sin} 5 \theta \text{sin} 3 \theta \text{d} \theta = 2 \left[\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4} + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{16}\right]`

**[M1]**

Write both terms over 16 before adding

`\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{6}} 4 \text{sin} 5 \theta \text{sin} 3 \theta \text{d} \theta = 2 \times \frac{5 \sqrt{3}}{16}`

`\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{6}} 4 \text{sin} 5 \theta \text{sin} 3 \theta \text{d} \theta = \frac{5 \sqrt{3}}{8}`

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Uses part (b) to write the integrand as a multiple of $\text{cos} 2 θ - \text{cos} 8 θ$, and integrates to obtain terms of the form $p \text{sin} 2 θ + q \text{sin} 8 θ$.
> 
> **A1**: A fully correct integral, `2 \left[\frac{\text{sin} 2 \theta}{2} - \frac{\text{sin} 8 \theta}{8}\right] + c` or any equivalent form such as $\text{sin} 2 θ - \frac{1}{4} \text{sin} 8 θ + c$.
> 
> **M1**: Substitutes both limits into your integrated expression and subtracts.
> 
> **A1**: $\frac{5\sqrt{3}}{8}$.
> 
> The constant of integration is required in the first sub-part but is not needed in the second.
> 
> Working in degrees is equally acceptable, provided the limits are converted, so the upper limit becomes $30 \circ$ and the two angles become $60 \circ$ and $240 \circ$.
> 
> The final answer must be exact, so $1 . 08$ earns nothing on the last mark.

> **[exam-tip]**
> A product of trigonometric functions is a signal to convert before integrating.
> 
> - There is no product rule for integration, so `\int \text{sin} 5 \theta \text{sin} 3 \theta \text{d} \theta` cannot be started directly
> - Parts (a) and (b) exist purely to hand you the sum form, so use them
> 
> Match the coefficient carefully when you reuse part (b).
> 
> - Part (b) converts $2 \text{sin} 5 x \text{sin} 3 x$, and the integrand here is $4 \text{sin} 5 θ \text{sin} 3 θ$, which is twice as big
> - Forgetting that factor of 2 halves the final answer
> 
> When integrating $\text{cos} k θ$, divide by $k$ rather than multiplying.
> 
> - `\int \text{cos} 8 \theta \text{d} \theta = \frac{\text{sin} 8 \theta}{8}`, so the term with the larger angle ends up the smaller
> - Differentiating your answer back is a quick way to check the divisions
> 
> The negative sine at the upper limit is where the answer grows rather than shrinks.
> 
> - $\frac{4π}{3}$ is in the third quadrant, so $\text{sin} \frac{4π}{3} = - \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$
> - Subtracting that negative value adds $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{16}$ on, which is what turns $\frac{4\sqrt{3}}{16}$ into $\frac{5\sqrt{3}}{16}$
> 
> Both limits still have to be substituted, even when one of them gives zero.
> 
> - Show the lower limit producing $\text{sin} 0 = 0$ rather than silently dropping it

parts.problemMd:
In triangle $ABC$, $AB$= $2x$cm, $BC=3x$ cm and $AC=4x$ cm

The area of triangle $ABC$ is $50$ cm<sup>2</sup>

Find, to 2 decimal places, the value of $x$
parts.solutionMd:
The area formula $\text{Area} = \frac{1}{2} a b \text{sin} C$ needs an angle, and the angle has to be the one between the two sides you use

No angle is given, so find one first

All three sides are known, which is exactly what the cosine rule needs

Take `\angle A B C`, the angle between $A B$ and $B C$, since $A C$ sits opposite it

`(4 x)^{2} = (2 x)^{2} + (3 x)^{2} - 2 \times 2 x \times 3 x \times \text{cos} \angle A B C`

**[M1]**

Every term carries $x^{2}$, so the $x$ divides out and the angle does not depend on $x$ at all

`16 x^{2} = 13 x^{2} - 12 x^{2} \text{cos} \angle A B C`

`3 x^{2} = - 12 x^{2} \text{cos} \angle A B C`

`\text{cos} \angle A B C = - \frac{1}{4}`

The cosine is negative, so this angle is obtuse

Use the identity $\text{sin}^{2} θ + \text{cos}^{2} θ \equiv 1$ to get the sine straight from the cosine, without ever working out the angle itself

The sine of an angle in a triangle is always positive, so take the positive root

`\text{sin} \angle A B C = \sqrt{1 - \left(- \frac{1}{4}\right)^{2}}`

`\text{sin} \angle A B C = \frac{\sqrt{15}}{4}`

**[A1]**

Now put that into the area formula, with $A B$ and $B C$ as the two sides and the area equal to 50

$50 = \frac{1}{2} \times 2 x \times 3 x \times \frac{\sqrt{15}}{4}$

$50 = \frac{3\sqrt{15}}{4} x^{2}$

$x^{2} = \frac{200}{3\sqrt{15}}$

$x^{2} = 17 . 213259 \dots$

**[M1]**

Take the positive square root, since $x$ is a length

$x = 4 . 148886 \dots$

$x=4.15(2d.p.)$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: A fully correct substitution into the cosine rule for any one of the three angles, or a fully correct rearranged expression for its cosine.
> 
> **A1**: A correct value for that angle, or a correct exact value for its sine or cosine.
> 
> **M1**: Substitutes your angle into $\text{Area} = \frac{1}{2} a b \text{sin} C$ with the two sides that enclose it, and reaches a value for $x^{2}$. This mark depends on the first method mark.
> 
> **A1**: $x = 4 . 15$. Accept answers which round to this value.
> 
> Any of the three angles may be chosen, provided the two sides in the area formula are the two that enclose it. Working in decimals rather than exact values is equally acceptable, and gives `\angle A B C = 104.47751 \ldots ^{\circ}`, `\angle B A C = 46.56746 \ldots ^{\circ}` or `\angle A C B = 28.95502 \ldots ^{\circ}`. All three routes reach $x^{2} = 17 . 213259 \dots$
> 
> The $x$ may be left out of the working throughout, or put back in at the end, and either is accepted.
> 
> Heron's formula is equally acceptable, and is marked like this. The first two marks are for $s = \frac{2x+3x+4x}{2}$ simplified to $\frac{9x}{2}$. The third mark is for substituting into $\text{Area} = \sqrt{s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)}$ and reaching $\sqrt{\frac{135x^{4}}{16}}$, and the fourth is for the same final value of $x$.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Three sides and no angle is the standard signal for the cosine rule.
> 
> - The area formula cannot start until you have an angle, so the cosine rule always comes first here
> - Rearranged, it gives you the cosine directly: $\text{cos} C = \frac{a^{2}+b^{2}-c^{2}}{2ab}$
> 
> Going from the cosine straight to the sine saves a rounding step.
> 
> - $\text{sin}^{2} θ + \text{cos}^{2} θ \equiv 1$ turns $- \frac{1}{4}$ into the exact value $\frac{\sqrt{15}}{4}$
> - Finding the angle first and then its sine works too, but store the full value in your calculator rather than rounding to $104 . 5 ^{\circ}$
> 
> The sides you use in the area formula must enclose the angle you found.
> 
> - `\angle A B C` sits between $A B$ and $B C$, so those are the two lengths that go in
> - Pairing an angle with the wrong two sides is the commonest way to lose the last two marks here
> 
> Every term in the cosine rule has an $x^{2}$ in it, which is worth noticing early.
> 
> - It means the angles of this triangle are fixed no matter what $x$ is, so only the area can pin $x$ down

parts.problemMd:
![Irregular hexagon with vertices A, B, C, D, E, F, and internal angles 60° and 45°. Diagram indicates "not accurately drawn." Side AB is 24 cm.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-further-maths-19/geometry-and-trigonometry/trigonometric-formulae-and-identities/assets/008-irregular-hexagon-with-vertices-a-b-c-d-e-f-and-.png)

Figure 5 shows a right triangular prism $ABCDEF$where $ABCD$ is a rectangle.

$AF=DEBF=CEAD=FE=BCAB=DC=24$ cm

`angle A B F space equals space angle D C E space equals space 45 degree     angle B A F space equals space angle C D E space equals 60 degree`

Using a formula from page 2,

show that $\mathrm{sin}AFB=\frac{\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{6}}{4}$
parts.solutionMd:
`\angle A F B` sits in triangle $A B F$, and the other two angles of that triangle are both given

The three angles of a triangle add to $180 ^{\circ}$

`\angle A F B = 180 ^{\circ} - 60 ^{\circ} - 45 ^{\circ}`

`\angle A F B = 75 ^{\circ}`

$75 ^{\circ}$ is not one of the standard exact angles, but it is the sum of two that are

Write it as $45 ^{\circ} + 30 ^{\circ}$ and use $\text{sin} ( A + B ) = \text{sin} A \text{cos} B + \text{cos} A \text{sin} B$ from the formulae sheet

$\text{sin} 75 ^{\circ} = \text{sin} 45 ^{\circ} \text{cos} 30 ^{\circ} + \text{cos} 45 ^{\circ} \text{sin} 30 ^{\circ}$

**[M1]**

Now put in the exact values

$\text{sin} 75 ^{\circ} = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \times \frac{1}{2}$

**[M1]**

$\sqrt{2} \times \sqrt{3} = \sqrt{6}$, so the two terms both end up over 4

$\text{sin} 75 ^{\circ} = \frac{\sqrt{6}}{4} + \frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}$

`\text{sin} \angle A F B = \frac{\sqrt{2} + \sqrt{6}}{4} \textrm{ }\text{as required}`

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Identifies `\angle A F B = 75 ^{\circ}` and uses a correct addition formula to split it. Accept $45 ^{\circ} + 30 ^{\circ}$, $120 ^{\circ} - 45 ^{\circ}$, or $60 ^{\circ} + 15 ^{\circ}$ with the half-angle values.
> 
> **M1**: Substitutes the correct exact values, shown explicitly.
> 
> **A1**: Reaches the given result with no errors.
> 
> The answer is given, so every step has to be shown. A calculator value of $0 . 9659$ earns nothing.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The exact angles are $30 ^{\circ}$, $45 ^{\circ}$ and $60 ^{\circ}$, and anything built from them is fair game.
> 
> - $75 ^{\circ} = 45 ^{\circ} + 30 ^{\circ}$, and $15 ^{\circ} = 45 ^{\circ} - 30 ^{\circ}$ works the same way
> - Whenever a question asks for a surd answer at an unusual angle, look for a sum or difference of two standard ones
> 
> Find the missing angle of the triangle before anything else.
> 
> - The question gives `\angle B A F = 60 ^{\circ}` and `\angle A B F = 45 ^{\circ}`, so `\angle A F B` follows in one line
> - It is easy to start reaching for the sine rule and miss that the angle is simply $180 ^{\circ}$ minus the other two
> 
> Write the exact values in before multiplying.
> 
> - Showing $\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ explicitly is worth a mark of its own here
> - Jumping straight to $\frac{\sqrt{6}}{4}$ risks the examiner not seeing where it came from

parts.problemMd:
Without using a calculator,

show that $B F  =  12 \left(3 \sqrt{2}  -  \sqrt{6}\right)$cm
parts.solutionMd:
$B F$ is opposite the $60 ^{\circ}$ angle and $A B$ is opposite the $75 ^{\circ}$ angle, so both are paired with a known angle

That is exactly what the sine rule needs

$\frac{BF}{\text{sin}60^{\circ}} = \frac{24}{\text{sin}75^{\circ}}$

**[M1]**

Substitute the exact values, taking $\text{sin} 75 ^{\circ}$ from part (a)

$\frac{BF}{\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}} = \frac{24}{\frac{\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{6}}{4}}$

**[M1]**

Dividing by a fraction means multiplying by its reciprocal

$B F = \frac{48\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{6}}$

**[A1]**

A surd in the denominator has to be cleared, so multiply top and bottom by $\sqrt{6} - \sqrt{2}$

$B F = \frac{48\sqrt{3}(\sqrt{6}-\sqrt{2})}{(\sqrt{6}+\sqrt{2})(\sqrt{6}-\sqrt{2})}$

**[M1]**

The denominator is a difference of two squares, so it becomes $6 - 2$

$B F = \frac{48\sqrt{18}-48\sqrt{6}}{4}$

$\sqrt{18} = 3 \sqrt{2}$, so the first term is $144 \sqrt{2}$

$B F = \frac{144\sqrt{2}-48\sqrt{6}}{4}$

$B F = 12 ( 3 \sqrt{2} - \sqrt{6} )  \text{cm as required}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: A correct sine rule statement pairing $B F$ with $60 ^{\circ}$ and 24 with $75 ^{\circ}$.
> 
> **M1**: Substitutes the exact values for both sines, using part (a).
> 
> **A1**: Reaches $\frac{48\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{6}}$ or an equivalent unrationalised form.
> 
> **M1**: Multiplies numerator and denominator by $\sqrt{6} - \sqrt{2}$ to rationalise.
> 
> **A1**: Reaches the given result with no errors.
> 
> The question says the calculator must not be used, so every surd manipulation has to be shown. A decimal such as $21 . 5$ appearing anywhere loses the final mark.
> 
> Rationalising by $\sqrt{2} - \sqrt{6}$ and adjusting the signs at the end is equally acceptable.

> **[exam-tip]**
> "Without using a calculator" tells you the answer will be a surd and the working is being marked.
> 
> - Every simplification has to appear on the page, including the difference of two squares in the denominator
> - A correct final answer with no visible surd work will not score the method marks
> 
> Part (a) is there so that you can substitute an exact value here.
> 
> - $\text{sin} 75 ^{\circ} = \frac{\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{6}}{4}$ is exactly what turns this into a surd calculation
> - Questions that prove a value and then use it are almost always signalling this
> 
> Rationalise by changing the sign between the two surds.
> 
> - $( \sqrt{6} + \sqrt{2} ) ( \sqrt{6} - \sqrt{2} ) = 6 - 2$, which is 4, and that is what clears the denominator
> - The order the two surds are written in does not matter, only that the sign flips
> 
> Watch $\sqrt{3} \times \sqrt{6}$.
> 
> - It is $\sqrt{18}$, which simplifies to $3 \sqrt{2}$, and that 3 is where the $3 \sqrt{2}$ in the answer comes from
> - Leaving it as $\sqrt{18}$ means the final form never matches the one printed in the question

parts.problemMd:
The angle between the plane $AEB$and the plane $ABCD$is $65^{\circ}$

Find, in cm to 2 significant figures, the length of $EF$
parts.solutionMd:
Plane $A E B$ and plane $A B C D$ meet along $A B$, so the angle between them is measured perpendicular to $A B$

Let $X$ be the point on $A B$ directly below $F$, and $Y$ the matching point on $D C$

Then $F X$ is the height of the triangular end above $A B$, and the required angle is `\angle E X Y`

Find $F X$ first, from the right-angled triangle $B F X$ with its $45 ^{\circ}$ angle at $B$

$F X = 12 ( 3 \sqrt{2} - \sqrt{6} ) \text{sin} 45 ^{\circ}$

**[M1]**

$F X = 36 - 12 \sqrt{3}$

$E$ sits directly behind $F$, so $E Y$ is the same height, and $X Y$ runs across the base with $X Y = E F$

Triangle $E X Y$ has its right angle at $Y$, with $E Y$ opposite the $65 ^{\circ}$ and $X Y$ adjacent to it

$\text{tan} 65 ^{\circ} = \frac{36-12\sqrt{3}}{EF}$

**[M1]**

$E F = \frac{36-12\sqrt{3}}{\text{tan}65^{\circ}}$

$E F = 7 . 09505 \dots$

$EF=7.1\text{cm}(2s.f.)$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: A correct method for the perpendicular height of $F$ above $A B$, giving $F X = 36 - 12 \sqrt{3}$, which is $15 . 2153 \dots$ as a decimal.
> 
> **M1**: A correct trigonometric statement linking your height, the $65 ^{\circ}$ angle and $E F$.
> 
> **A1**: Accept answers which round to $7 . 1$ cm.
> 
> Finding $F X$ from the area of triangle $A B F$ is equally acceptable, since $\frac{1}{2} \times 24 \times F X$ must equal $\frac{1}{2} \times 24 \times B F \times \text{sin} 45 ^{\circ}$.
> 
> Using $A F$ and the $60 ^{\circ}$ angle at $A$ instead reaches the same height and is equally acceptable.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The angle between two planes is measured along a line perpendicular to where they meet.
> 
> - The planes meet along $A B$, so both arms of the angle must be at right angles to $A B$
> - $X Y$ lies in the base and $X E$ lies in the plane $A E B$, which is what makes `\angle E X Y` the one you want
> 
> The height of the triangular end is the quantity that links every part of this question.
> 
> - $F X = 36 - 12 \sqrt{3}$ comes straight out of part (b) and is used again in part (d)
> - Store it in your calculator rather than rounding to $15 . 2$
> 
> $E F$ is the depth of the prism, not a slant length.
> 
> - $E F$ equals $A D$ and $B C$, and it lies flat in the base, which is why it is the adjacent side here
> - The prism is right, so every one of those edges is perpendicular to the triangular ends
> 
> Two significant figures is a low precision, so do not round early.
> 
> - The unrounded $7 . 09505$ rounds cleanly to $7 . 1$
> - Rounding $\text{tan} 65 ^{\circ}$ or the height first can push a borderline answer the wrong way

parts.problemMd: Find, in degrees to one decimal place, the size of the angle between the line $CF$and the plane $ABCD$
parts.solutionMd:
The angle between a line and a plane is the angle between the line and its shadow on that plane

$X$ is the point directly below $F$, so the shadow of $C F$ on the base is $C X$

**Final answer:** **The required angle is **`\angle F C X`

**[B1]**

To use that angle, find $C F$ first

$C$ is directly behind $B$ by the depth of the prism, and that depth is perpendicular to $B F$

So $B F$ and $E F$ are two sides of a right angle, with $C F$ as the hypotenuse

`C F = \sqrt{[12 (3 \sqrt{2} - \sqrt{6})]^{2} + 7.09505 \ldots^{2}}`

**[M1]**

$C F = 22 . 6573 \dots$

Triangle $F X C$ has its right angle at $X$, with $F X$ opposite the angle at $C$ and $C F$ as the hypotenuse

`\text{sin} \angle F C X = \frac{15.2153 \ldots}{22.6573 \ldots}`

**[M1]**

`\angle F C X = 42.186 \ldots ^{\circ}`

$\angle F C X = 42 . 2 \circ  \left(1 d . p .\right)$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Identifies the required angle as `\angle F C X`, where $X$ is the point on $A B$ directly below $F$.
> 
> **M1**: A correct method for $C F$, using Pythagoras with your $B F$ and your $E F$.
> 
> **M1**: A correct trigonometric statement for the angle, using your height and your $C F$.
> 
> **A1**: Accept answers which round to $42 . 2 ^{\circ}$.
> 
> Follow through from your value of $E F$ in part (c).
> 
> Working through the horizontal distance $C X$ instead is equally acceptable, giving `\text{tan} \angle F C X = \frac{15.2153 \ldots}{16.7883 \ldots}` and the same angle.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Name the angle before you calculate anything.
> 
> - There is a mark here purely for identifying `\angle F C X`, and it is available even if the arithmetic goes wrong
> - Dropping the perpendicular from $F$ to the base is what creates the right-angled triangle you need
> 
> $C F$ is a diagonal across the prism, so it takes two steps.
> 
> - $B F$ is the sloping edge of the triangular end, and $B C$ is the depth, and the two are perpendicular
> - So $C F^{2} = B F^{2} + B C^{2}$, with $B C = E F$ from part (c)
> 
> The height is the same one you found in part (c).
> 
> - $F X = 36 - 12 \sqrt{3}$ has now been used three times, in parts (b), (c) and (d)
> - Recognising a repeated quantity saves time and keeps the rounding consistent
> 
> Choose the ratio that uses the lengths you already have.
> 
> - $F X$ and $C F$ are known, and they are opposite and hypotenuse, so the sine is the natural choice
> - Working out $C X$ first and using the tangent also works, but it is an extra calculation for no gain

parts.problemMd:
Using [formulae ](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2026/02/33569-EDX%20IGCSE%20Further%20Pure%20Maths%20Formulae%20Sheet.pdf), show that

(i) $\mathrm{cos}2A=2\mathrm{cos}^{2}A-1$

(3)

(ii) $\mathrm{sin}2A=2\mathrm{sin}A\mathrm{cos}A$

(1)
parts.solutionMd:
**(i)**

A double angle is an angle added to itself, so start from the addition formula on the formulae sheet

Use $\text{cos} ( A + B ) = \text{cos} A \text{cos} B - \text{sin} A \text{sin} B$ with both angles equal to $A$

$\text{cos} 2 A = \text{cos}^{2} A - \text{sin}^{2} A$

**[M1]**

The target has only cosines in it, so remove the sine using $\text{sin}^{2} A + \text{cos}^{2} A \equiv 1$

$\text{cos} 2 A = \text{cos}^{2} A - ( 1 - \text{cos}^{2} A )$

**[M1]**

Remove the bracket and collect the two cosine terms

$\text{cos} 2 A = 2 \text{cos}^{2} A - 1  \text{as required}$

**[A1]**

**(ii)**

Do the same with the sine addition formula, $\text{sin} ( A + B ) = \text{sin} A \text{cos} B + \text{cos} A \text{sin} B$

$\text{sin} 2 A = \text{sin} A \text{cos} A + \text{cos} A \text{sin} A$

The two terms are the same product written the other way round, so they add

$\text{sin} 2 A = 2 \text{sin} A \text{cos} A  \text{as required}$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of the addition formula for $\text{cos} ( A + A )$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of $\text{sin}^{2} A + \text{cos}^{2} A \equiv 1$ to eliminate $\text{sin}^{2} A$.
> 
> **A1**: Reaches the first given result with no errors.
> 
> **B1**: A complete derivation of the second given result from the addition formula for $\text{sin} ( A + A )$.
> 
> Both answers are given, so both derivations must be complete.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The formulae sheet gives the addition formulae, not the double angle ones.
> 
> - Setting $B = A$ in $\text{cos} ( A + B )$ and $\text{sin} ( A + B )$ is what produces them
> - That is why these two derivations appear so often as opening parts
> 
> The sine version needs one step and the cosine version needs two.
> 
> - $\text{sin} 2 A$ is finished as soon as you collect the two identical products
> - $\text{cos} 2 A = \text{cos}^{2} A - \text{sin}^{2} A$ is correct but not the required form, so the Pythagorean identity has to follow
> 
> These two results are the engine for the rest of the question.
> 
> - Part (b) builds $\text{cos} 3 A$ out of both of them
> - Part (d) then uses part (b) to integrate a cube, which cannot be integrated directly

parts.problemMd: Show that $\mathrm{cos}^{3}A=\frac{\mathrm{cos}3A+3\mathrm{cos}A}{4}$
parts.solutionMd:
A triple angle is a double angle plus a single one, so split $3 A$ that way and use the cosine addition formula

$\text{cos} 3 A = \text{cos} 2 A \text{cos} A - \text{sin} 2 A \text{sin} A$

**[M1]**

Now substitute both results from part (a)

$\text{cos} 3 A = ( 2 \text{cos}^{2} A - 1 ) \text{cos} A - 2 \text{sin} A \text{cos} A \text{sin} A$

**[M1]**

Expand the first bracket, and write the two sines as a square

$\text{cos} 3 A = 2 \text{cos}^{3} A - \text{cos} A - 2 \text{sin}^{2} A \text{cos} A$

There is still a sine in the expression, so remove it with $\text{sin}^{2} A + \text{cos}^{2} A \equiv 1$

$\text{cos} 3 A = 2 \text{cos}^{3} A - \text{cos} A - 2 ( 1 - \text{cos}^{2} A ) \text{cos} A$

Expand that bracket, taking care with the two minus signs

$\text{cos} 3 A = 2 \text{cos}^{3} A - \text{cos} A - 2 \text{cos} A + 2 \text{cos}^{3} A$

Collect the cubes and collect the single cosines

$\text{cos} 3 A = 4 \text{cos}^{3} A - 3 \text{cos} A$

**[M1]**

Rearrange to make $\text{cos}^{3} A$ the subject

$4 \text{cos}^{3} A = \text{cos} 3 A + 3 \text{cos} A$

$\text{cos}^{3} A = \frac{\text{cos}3A+3\text{cos}A}{4}  \text{as required}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Writes $\text{cos} 3 A$ as $\text{cos} ( 2 A + A )$ and expands correctly with the addition formula.
> 
> **M1**: Substitutes both results from part (a).
> 
> **M1**: Uses $\text{sin}^{2} A + \text{cos}^{2} A \equiv 1$ and simplifies to $4 \text{cos}^{3} A - 3 \text{cos} A$.
> 
> **A1**: Rearranges to the given result with no errors.
> 
> Starting from the right-hand side and working back to the left is equally acceptable, and carries the same four marks in the same order.
> 
> Splitting $3 A$ as $A + 2 A$ rather than $2 A + A$ is also equally acceptable.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Any multiple angle can be broken down into ones you already have.
> 
> - $3 A = 2 A + A$ turns an unfamiliar triple angle into an addition formula plus the two results from part (a)
> - The same trick handles $4 A$ as $2 A + 2 A$, and so on
> 
> Expect to use the Pythagorean identity a second time.
> 
> - Substituting part (a) leaves a $\text{sin}^{2} A$ term behind, and the target has no sines in it at all
> - Whenever a proof is meant to end in one function only, that identity is how you get there
> 
> Watch the double minus in the expansion.
> 
> - $- 2 ( 1 - \text{cos}^{2} A ) \text{cos} A$ gives $- 2 \text{cos} A + 2 \text{cos}^{3} A$
> - Getting that sign wrong gives $- 3 \text{cos}^{3} A$ instead of $4 \text{cos}^{3} A$, and the proof will not close
> 
> This result is what makes parts (c) and (d) possible.
> 
> - A cubed cosine cannot be solved for or integrated directly, but a sum of ordinary cosines can
> - Reading ahead to see what the later parts need is a good way to understand why a proof is being asked for

parts.problemMd:
Hence, or otherwise, solve, giving exact values in terms of $π$

$8  cos^{3}  \left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)  -  6  cos  \left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)  -  1  =  0$   for `0 space less-than or slanted equal to space theta space less-than or slanted equal to space 2 straight pi`
parts.solutionMd:
The equation contains a cubed cosine and an ordinary cosine of the same angle, which is exactly the shape part (b) deals with

Part (b) rearranges to $4 \text{cos}^{3} A = \text{cos} 3 A + 3 \text{cos} A$, so doubling it gives the $8 \text{cos}^{3} A$ the equation needs

$8 \text{cos}^{3} A = 2 \text{cos} 3 A + 6 \text{cos} A$

Here the angle playing the part of $A$ is $\frac{θ}{2}$, so $3 A$ becomes $\frac{3θ}{2}$

Substitute into the equation

$2 \text{cos} \frac{3θ}{2} + 6 \text{cos} \frac{θ}{2} - 6 \text{cos} \frac{θ}{2} - 1 = 0$

**[M1]**

The two $\text{cos} \frac{θ}{2}$ terms cancel, which is the whole point of the substitution

$2 \text{cos} \frac{3θ}{2} = 1$

$\text{cos} \frac{3θ}{2} = \frac{1}{2}$

**[M1]**

Solve for $\frac{3θ}{2}$ rather than $θ$, and scale the range to match

Since $0 \leq θ \leq 2 π$, the angle $\frac{3θ}{2}$ runs from $0$ to $3 π$

The cosine is $\frac{1}{2}$ at $\frac{π}{3}$, and then at $\frac{π}{3}$ either side of every multiple of $2 π$

$\frac{3θ}{2} = \frac{π}{3} , \frac{5π}{3} , \frac{7π}{3}$

**[M1]**

The next one would be $\frac{11π}{3}$, which is beyond $3 π$

Multiply each value by $\frac{2}{3}$ to get back to $θ$

$θ = \frac{2π}{9} , \frac{10π}{9} , \frac{14π}{9}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Uses part (b) to replace `8 \text{cos}^{3} \left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)` by $2 \text{cos} \frac{3θ}{2} + 6 \text{cos} \frac{θ}{2}$.
> 
> **M1**: Rearranges to $\text{cos} \frac{3θ}{2} = \frac{1}{2}$.
> 
> **M1**: Finds at least one correct value for $\frac{3θ}{2}$, having scaled the range to $0 \leq \frac{3θ}{2} \leq 3 π$.
> 
> **A1**: All three values of $θ$, and no extra values inside the range.
> 
> The question asks for exact values in terms of $π$, so decimal answers earn nothing on the final mark.
> 
> Working in degrees throughout is equally acceptable, provided the answers are converted back, giving $40 ^{\circ}$, $200 ^{\circ}$ and $280 ^{\circ}$.

> **[exam-tip]**
> "Hence, or otherwise" is a strong hint that the previous part does most of the work.
> 
> - Without part (b) this is a cubic in `\text{cos} \left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)` with no obvious factorisation
> - With it, the whole equation collapses to a single cosine in two lines
> 
> The angle inside the cosine is $\frac{θ}{2}$, so the identity's $3 A$ becomes $\frac{3θ}{2}$.
> 
> - Substituting $A = \frac{θ}{2}$ carefully is where most of the difficulty in this part sits
> - Writing $A = \frac{θ}{2}$ down explicitly before you start is worth the line
> 
> Scale the range by exactly the same factor as the angle.
> 
> - $θ$ becoming $\frac{3θ}{2}$ multiplies the range by $\frac{3}{2}$, so $2 π$ becomes $3 π$
> - That wider range is why there are three answers rather than two, and stopping early is the usual error
> 
> The cosine takes each value twice per revolution.
> 
> - $\text{cos} x = \frac{1}{2}$ at $\frac{π}{3}$ and at $2 π - \frac{π}{3} = \frac{5π}{3}$, then repeats every $2 π$
> - Listing the values of $\frac{3θ}{2}$ first and scaling at the end is far safer than scaling as you go

parts.problemMd:
Use algebraic integration to find the exact value of

$\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{6}} \left(4  cos^{3}  \theta  -  sin  2 \theta\right)  d \theta$
parts.solutionMd:
A cubed cosine cannot be integrated directly, so use part (b) to turn it into a sum of ordinary cosines

Multiplying part (b) by 4 gives $4 \text{cos}^{3} θ = \text{cos} 3 θ + 3 \text{cos} θ$

Call the integral $I$

`I = \int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{6}} \left(\text{cos} 3 \theta + 3 \text{cos} \theta - \text{sin} 2 \theta\right) \text{d} \theta`

**[M1]**

Integrate term by term, dividing by the multiple of $θ$ inside each function

Note that integrating $- \text{sin} 2 θ$ gives $+ \frac{\text{cos}2θ}{2}$, because the minus signs cancel

`I = \left[\frac{\text{sin} 3 \theta}{3} + 3 \text{sin} \theta + \frac{\text{cos} 2 \theta}{2}\right]_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{6}}`

**[M1]**

At the upper limit the three angles are $\frac{π}{2}$, $\frac{π}{6}$ and $\frac{π}{3}$, all with exact values

$\frac{\text{sin}\frac{π}{2}}{3} + 3 \text{sin} \frac{π}{6} + \frac{\text{cos}\frac{π}{3}}{2} = \frac{1}{3} + \frac{3}{2} + \frac{1}{4}$

$\frac{1}{3} + \frac{3}{2} + \frac{1}{4} = \frac{25}{12}$

At the lower limit both sines are zero, but the cosine term is not

$\frac{\text{sin}0}{3} + 3 \text{sin} 0 + \frac{\text{cos}0}{2} = \frac{1}{2}$

Subtract the lower value from the upper one

$I = \frac{25}{12} - \frac{1}{2}$

**[M1]**

$I = \frac{19}{12}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Replaces $4 \text{cos}^{3} θ$ by $\text{cos} 3 θ + 3 \text{cos} θ$ using part (b).
> 
> **M1**: Integrates to obtain terms of the form $p \text{sin} 3 θ + q \text{sin} θ + r \text{cos} 2 θ$.
> 
> **M1**: Substitutes both limits into your integrated expression and subtracts.
> 
> **A1**: $\frac{19}{12}$.
> 
> The lower limit does not vanish here, because $\text{cos} 0 = 1$. Dropping it gives $\frac{25}{12}$ and loses the final mark.
> 
> The question asks for an exact value, so $1 . 58$ earns nothing on the last mark.

> **[exam-tip]**
> A power of a trigonometric function is a signal to convert before integrating.
> 
> - There is no rule for integrating $\text{cos}^{3} θ$ as it stands
> - Every part of this question has been building towards this moment, so use part (b) rather than starting again
> 
> Two sign changes are easy to lose here.
> 
> - Integrating $- \text{sin} 2 θ$ gives $+ \frac{\text{cos}2θ}{2}$, since the integral of $\text{sin}$ is $- \text{cos}$
> - Differentiating your integrated expression back is the quickest way to check both the signs and the divisions
> 
> Never assume the lower limit contributes nothing.
> 
> - Two of the three terms do vanish at $θ = 0$, but $\frac{\text{cos}0}{2} = \frac{1}{2}$ does not
> - Writing out the lower bracket in full, even when most of it is zero, is what stops this being missed
> 
> Keep everything as fractions.
> 
> - The answer is exact, so $\frac{1}{3} + \frac{3}{2} + \frac{1}{4}$ should be put over 12 rather than turned into decimals
> - A common denominator at the end is much safer than rounding at each step

parts.problemMd:
Triangle $ABC$is such that

$AC=10\mathrm{cm}BC=7\mathrm{cm} \mathrm{angle}CAB=25^{\circ}$

Given that angle $ABC$is obtuse,

find, in cm to one decimal place, the length of $AB$
parts.solutionMd:
You have an angle and the side opposite it, plus one more side, so the sine rule is the tool to reach for

$B C = 7$ is opposite `\angle C A B = 25 ^{\circ}`, and $A C = 10$ is opposite `\angle A B C`

`\frac{\text{sin} 25 ^{\circ}}{7} = \frac{\text{sin} \angle A B C}{10}`

**[M1]**

Rearrange to find the sine of the angle at $B$

`\text{sin} \angle A B C = \frac{10 \text{sin} 25 ^{\circ}}{7}`

`\text{sin} \angle A B C = 0.603740 \ldots`

The calculator gives only the acute angle, but there is a second angle in the range with the same sine, found by subtracting from $180 ^{\circ}$

`\angle A B C = 37.138 \ldots ^{\circ} \text{ or } 142.861 \ldots ^{\circ}`

**[M1]**

The question says `\angle A B C` is obtuse, so the second of these is the one to take

The three angles of a triangle add to $180 ^{\circ}$

`\angle A C B = 180 ^{\circ} - 25 ^{\circ} - 142.861 \ldots ^{\circ}`

`\angle A C B = 12.138 \ldots ^{\circ}`

**[A1]**

$A B$ is opposite `\angle A C B`, so use the sine rule once more, pairing it with the side and angle you were given

$\frac{AB}{\text{sin}12.138\dots^{\circ}} = \frac{7}{\text{sin}25^{\circ}}$

$A B = \frac{7\text{sin}12.138\dots^{\circ}}{\text{sin}25^{\circ}}$

**[M1]**

$A B = 3 . 4829 \dots$

$AB=3.5\text{cm}(1d.p.)$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: A fully correct substitution into the sine rule.
> 
> **M1**: A correct rearrangement to find `\angle A B C`, which may be implied by either the correct acute or the correct obtuse angle appearing. This mark depends on the first method mark.
> 
> **A1**: `\angle A C B` found. Accept angles which round to $12$.
> 
> **M1**: A correct substitution into either the sine rule or the cosine rule using your angles. This mark depends on both earlier method marks.
> 
> **A1**: Accept answers which round to $3 . 5$ cm.
> 
> The acute angle $37 . 138 \dots ^{\circ}$ may be used throughout instead, provided `\angle A C B` is then taken as $180 ^{\circ} - 25 ^{\circ} - 37 . 138 \dots ^{\circ} = 117 . 861 \dots ^{\circ}$ and the final answer is the same.
> 
> The cosine rule is equally acceptable as a complete alternative, and is marked like this. Substituting into $7^{2} = 10^{2} + A B^{2} - 2 \times 10 \times A B \times \text{cos} 25 ^{\circ}$ earns the first mark, rearranging it to $A B^{2} - 20 A B \text{cos} 25 ^{\circ} + 51 = 0$ earns the second, and the correct three-term quadratic earns the third. A genuine attempt to solve it earns the fourth, and the fifth is for $3 . 5$ cm with the second root, $14 . 64$, rejected.
> 
> Splitting the triangle with a perpendicular is also equally acceptable, and is marked like this. The first two marks are as in the main scheme. Finding $A X = 10 \text{cos} 25 ^{\circ}$, which is $9 . 06 \dots$, earns the third, a correct method for $B X$ and hence $A B$ earns the fourth, and $3 . 5$ cm earns the fifth.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The word "obtuse" in the question is the whole point of it.
> 
> - A sine is positive for both an acute angle and its supplement, so $\text{sin} 37 . 14 ^{\circ}$ and $\text{sin} 142 . 86 ^{\circ}$ are equal
> - Your calculator only ever returns the acute one, so you have to produce the other yourself by subtracting from $180 ^{\circ}$
> 
> This is the ambiguous case of the sine rule, and it appears whenever you are given two sides and an angle that is not between them.
> 
> - The tell is that the side opposite the given angle is shorter than the other given side, here 7 against 10
> - Two genuinely different triangles fit the information, and the question picks one for you
> 
> Keep the unrounded angle in your calculator.
> 
> - Rounding `\angle A C B` to $12 ^{\circ}$ before the last step gives $3 . 44$ cm, which does not round to $3 . 5$
> - Store the value in a memory rather than retyping it
> 
> A quick sanity check is worth the few seconds.
> 
> - The obtuse angle at $B$ leaves very little of the triangle for the angle at $C$, so $A B$ should come out short
> - An answer of $14 . 6$ cm is the other triangle, the one with an acute angle at $B$

parts.problemMd:
Using a [formula ](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2026/02/33569-EDX%20IGCSE%20Further%20Pure%20Maths%20Formulae%20Sheet.pdf), show that

$\mathrm{tan}2A=\frac{2\mathrm{tan}A}{1-\mathrm{tan}^{2}A}$
parts.solutionMd:
The formulae sheet gives the addition formula for tangent, and a double angle is just an angle added to itself

Write $2 A$ as $A + A$, then use $\text{tan} ( A + B ) = \frac{\text{tan}A+\text{tan}B}{1-\text{tan}A\text{tan}B}$ with $B$ replaced by $A$

$\text{tan} 2 A = \frac{\text{tan}A+\text{tan}A}{1-\text{tan}A\text{tan}A}$

**[M1]**

Collect the two identical terms on the top, and write the product on the bottom as a square

$\text{tan} 2 A = \frac{2\text{tan}A}{1-\text{tan}^{2}A}  \text{as required}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Writes $\text{tan} 2 A$ as $\text{tan} ( A + A )$ and substitutes into the addition formula, reaching $\frac{\text{tan}A+\text{tan}A}{1-\text{tan}A\text{tan}A}$.
> 
> **A1**: Simplifies to the given result with no errors or omitted steps.
> 
> The answer is given, so the working must be complete. Simply quoting the double angle formula earns nothing, since quoting it is what the question asks you to prove.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Every double angle formula comes from an addition formula with the two angles made equal.
> 
> - $\text{tan} 2 A = \text{tan} ( A + A )$ is the whole idea, and the same trick gives the sine and cosine versions
> - The formulae sheet has the addition formulae, so you never have to remember the double angle ones separately
> 
> Show both simplifications separately.
> 
> - $\text{tan} A + \text{tan} A$ becoming $2 \text{tan} A$ and $\text{tan} A \text{tan} A$ becoming $\text{tan}^{2} A$ are two different steps
> - On a two-mark "show that" the accuracy mark is for exactly this kind of completeness

parts.problemMd:
Hence, solve the equation

$\mathrm{tan}A^{\circ}-\mathrm{tan}2A^{\circ}=0$              for `0 less-than or slanted equal to A less-than or slanted equal to 180`
parts.solutionMd:
"Hence" means part (a) is the way in, so substitute the result you have just proved

$\text{tan} A - \frac{2\text{tan}A}{1-\text{tan}^{2}A} = 0$

**[M1]**

Clear the fraction by multiplying every term by $1 - \text{tan}^{2} A$

$\text{tan} A ( 1 - \text{tan}^{2} A ) - 2 \text{tan} A = 0$

**[M1]**

Expand the bracket

$\text{tan} A - \text{tan}^{3} A - 2 \text{tan} A = 0$

Collect the two $\text{tan} A$ terms

$- \text{tan}^{3} A - \text{tan} A = 0$

Multiply through by $- 1$ to make the leading term positive

$\text{tan}^{3} A + \text{tan} A = 0$

Every term has a factor of $\text{tan} A$, so factorise rather than dividing by it, since dividing would lose solutions

$\text{tan} A ( \text{tan}^{2} A + 1 ) = 0$

**[M1]**

A product is zero when one of its factors is zero, so consider each in turn

The second factor gives $\text{tan}^{2} A = - 1$, and no square can be negative, so that factor produces nothing

$\text{tan} A = 0$

$A = 0$

**[A1]**

The tangent graph repeats every $180 ^{\circ}$, so add $180$ to reach the only other value in range

$A=0,180$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correctly substitutes the result of part (a) into the given equation.
> 
> **M1**: Multiplies through by $1 - \text{tan}^{2} A$, or reaches a correct single fraction and eliminates $1 - \text{tan}^{2} A$ as the denominator.
> 
> **M1**: A correct rearrangement of your equation, factorised correctly into a linear factor and a quadratic factor equal to zero.
> 
> **A1**: Either $A = 0$ or $A = 180$. This mark depends on all three method marks.
> 
> **A1**: Both $A = 0$ and $A = 180$, with no other values inside the range. Values outside the range are ignored. This mark depends on all three method marks.
> 
> An answer reached by trial and improvement scores nothing on this question, however many correct values it lists.
> 
> Working from a correct single fraction is equally acceptable, so `\text{tan} A \left(1 - \frac{2}{1 - \text{tan}^{2} A}\right) = 0` leading to $1 - \text{tan}^{2} A - 2 = 0$ earns the second and third marks.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Factorise rather than divide, or you will lose the solutions you are being asked for.
> 
> - Cancelling $\text{tan} A$ from $\text{tan}^{3} A + \text{tan} A = 0$ throws away $\text{tan} A = 0$, which is where both answers come from
> - The habit to build is that a trigonometric equation equal to zero always wants factorising
> 
> A quadratic factor with no real roots is still worth a line of writing.
> 
> - $\text{tan}^{2} A + 1 = 0$ needs $\text{tan}^{2} A = - 1$, which is impossible for a real angle
> - Say so explicitly rather than ignoring the factor, so the examiner can see you considered it
> 
> Check the endpoints of the range carefully.
> 
> - The range here is $0 \leq A \leq 180$ and both ends are included, so $0$ and $180$ both count
> - A range written with strict inequalities would have left this equation with no solutions at all
> 
> Note where the equation is undefined.
> 
> - $\text{tan} 90 ^{\circ}$ does not exist, so $A = 90$ could never be a solution whatever the algebra suggested
> - Neither of the answers is affected here, but it is worth a glance on any question involving tangents

parts.problemMd:
Using a formula given on page 2, solve, giving your solutions as exact values

$cos \left(x - \frac{\pi}{6}\right) = sin x$        for `negative pi less-than or slanted equal to x less-than or slanted equal to 2 pi`
parts.solutionMd:
The angles on the two sides are different, so expand the compound angle to get everything in terms of $x$

The formulae sheet gives $\text{cos} ( A - B ) = \text{cos} A \text{cos} B + \text{sin} A \text{sin} B$

$\text{cos} x \text{cos} \frac{π}{6} + \text{sin} x \text{sin} \frac{π}{6} = \text{sin} x$

**[M1]**

$\text{cos} \frac{π}{6} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ and $\text{sin} \frac{π}{6} = \frac{1}{2}$, both exact values worth knowing

$\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \text{cos} x + \frac{1}{2} \text{sin} x = \text{sin} x$

Multiply through by 2 to clear the fractions

$\sqrt{3} \text{cos} x + \text{sin} x = 2 \text{sin} x$

$\sqrt{3} \text{cos} x = \text{sin} x$

Divide both sides by $\text{cos} x$, using $\text{tan} x = \frac{\text{sin}x}{\text{cos}x}$

$\text{tan} x = \sqrt{3}$

**[M1]**

$\sqrt{3}$ is an exact value, so the base angle is one to recognise rather than look up

$x = \frac{π}{3}$

**[A1]**

The tangent graph repeats every $π$, so subtract $π$ and add $π$ to sweep the whole range $- π \leq x \leq 2 π$

Adding $π$ twice would give $\frac{7π}{3}$, which is outside the range

$x=-\frac{2π}{3},\frac{π}{3},\frac{4π}{3}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Uses the formula for $\text{cos} ( A - B )$ to expand the left-hand side correctly.
> 
> **M1**: Rearranges to $\text{tan} x = \sqrt{3}$, or to $\text{tan} x = a$ for their value of $a$. This mark depends on the first method mark.
> 
> **A1**: One correct value in range.
> 
> **A1**: All three correct values, and no extra values inside the range.
> 
> The question asks for exact values, so decimal answers such as $1 . 05$ earn nothing on the final two marks.
> 
> Working in degrees and converting back is equally acceptable, giving $60 ^{\circ}$, and the range becomes $- 180 ^{\circ} \leq x \leq 360 ^{\circ}$.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Different angles on the two sides always means expanding first.
> 
> - You cannot compare `\text{cos} \left(x - \frac{\pi}{6}\right)` with $\text{sin} x$ until both are written in terms of $x$ alone
> - Once expanded, the sine terms collect and the equation collapses to a tangent
> 
> Dividing by $\text{cos} x$ is safe here, but it is worth knowing why.
> 
> - If $\text{cos} x$ were zero then $\sqrt{3} \text{cos} x = \text{sin} x$ would force $\text{sin} x = 0$ too, and they are never both zero
> - So no solutions are lost, unlike the factorising situation in part (b)
> 
> Count how many solutions the range should hold before you write any down.
> 
> - The range $- π \leq x \leq 2 π$ is three lots of $π$ wide and $\text{tan}$ repeats every $π$, so expect three answers
> - Getting only one is the commonest way to lose the last mark here
> 
> Exact values mean surds and multiples of $π$ throughout.
> 
> - $\text{tan} x = \sqrt{3}$ gives $\frac{π}{3}$ exactly, so there is never a need for the calculator
> - Keep the answers as fractions of $π$ rather than converting to decimals at the end

parts.problemMd:
![Geometric diagram with triangle OAB and line CD intersecting at C. Labelled points: O, A, B, C, and D. Note states: "Diagram NOT accurately drawn."](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-further-maths-19/geometry-and-trigonometry/trigonometric-formulae-and-identities/assets/005-geometric-diagram-with-triangle-oab-and-line-cd-.png)

Figure 2 shows triangle $AOB$

$\overset{\rightarrow}{OA}=4a+5b\overset{\rightarrow}{OB}=8a-b\overset{\rightarrow}{OD}=15a+10b$      where $\left|\mathbf{a}\right| = \left|\mathbf{b}\right| = 1$

(i) Find $\overset{\rightarrow}{AB}$ in terms of $a$ and $b$

[2]

(ii) Find, in its simplest form, the exact value of $\left|\overset{\rightarrow}{A B}\right|$

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
**(i)**

There is no direct route from $A$ to $B$ in the information given, so travel through $O$

Go backwards along $\overset{\rightarrow}{OA}$ and then forwards along $\overset{\rightarrow}{OB}$

$\overset{\rightarrow}{AB} = \overset{\rightarrow}{AO} + \overset{\rightarrow}{OB}$

Reversing a vector reverses its sign, so $\overset{\rightarrow}{AO} = - ( 4 a + 5 b )$

$\overset{\rightarrow}{AB} = - 4 a - 5 b + 8 a - b$

**[M1]**

Collect the $a$ terms and the $b$ terms separately

$\overset{\rightarrow}{AB} = 4 a - 6 b$

**[A1]**

**(ii)**

$a$ and $b$ are perpendicular unit vectors, so the two components are at right angles and Pythagoras gives the length

`\left|\overset{\rightarrow}{A B}\right| = \sqrt{4^{2} + (- 6)^{2}}`

`\left|\overset{\rightarrow}{A B}\right| = \sqrt{52}`

The question asks for the simplest form, and $52 = 4 \times 13$

`\left|\overset{\rightarrow}{A B}\right| = 2 \sqrt{13}`

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: A correct vector path to find $\overset{\rightarrow}{AB}$ or $\overset{\rightarrow}{BA}$, so $\pm ( - 4 a - 5 b + 8 a - b )$.
> 
> **A1**: $\overset{\rightarrow}{AB} = 4 a - 6 b$.
> 
> **B1**: The exact magnitude in its simplest form, $2 \sqrt{13}$.
> 
> $\sqrt{52}$ on its own does not earn the final mark, because the question asks for the simplest form.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Build any missing vector by walking a path through points you do know.
> 
> - $\overset{\rightarrow}{AB} = \overset{\rightarrow}{AO} + \overset{\rightarrow}{OB}$ works because the middle letters match up and cancel
> - $\overset{\rightarrow}{AO}$ is not given, but it is just $\overset{\rightarrow}{OA}$ with every sign reversed
> 
> Watch the sign on the single $b$.
> 
> - $\overset{\rightarrow}{OB} = 8 a - b$ contributes $- b$, and $- 5 b - b = - 6 b$
> - A coefficient of 1 written invisibly is one of the easiest things to drop
> 
> Simplify the surd before you stop.
> 
> - $52 = 4 \times 13$, so the surd simplifies to $2 \sqrt{13}$, and the mark here is specifically for the simplified form
> - Look for the largest square factor rather than the first one you spot
> 
> Keep $\sqrt{52}$ to hand for part (b).
> 
> - It is one of the three side lengths of the triangle, so you will want it again in a moment
> - Using the unsimplified form there keeps the cosine rule arithmetic tidier

parts.problemMd:
![Triangle OAB with intersecting line OCD. Points A, B, C, D, and O labelled. Note states diagram is not accurately drawn.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-further-maths-19/geometry-and-trigonometry/trigonometric-formulae-and-identities/assets/006-triangle-oab-with-intersecting-line-ocd-points-a.png)

Figure 2 shows triangle $AOB$

$\overset{\rightarrow}{OA}=4a+5b\overset{\rightarrow}{OB}=8a-b\overset{\rightarrow}{OD}=15a+10b$      where $\left|\mathbf{a}\right| = \left|\mathbf{b}\right| = 1$

Find the area of triangle $AOB$
parts.solutionMd:
The area formula $\text{Area} = \frac{1}{2} a b \text{sin} C$ needs two sides and the angle between them

The two sides from $O$ are $\overset{\rightarrow}{OA}$ and $\overset{\rightarrow}{OB}$, so find their lengths first

`\left|\overset{\rightarrow}{O A}\right| = \sqrt{4^{2} + 5^{2}}`

`\left|\overset{\rightarrow}{O A}\right| = \sqrt{41}`

`\left|\overset{\rightarrow}{O B}\right| = \sqrt{8^{2} + (- 1)^{2}}`

`\left|\overset{\rightarrow}{O B}\right| = \sqrt{65}`

**[M1]**

Part (a) already gives the third side, `\left|\overset{\rightarrow}{A B}\right| = \sqrt{52}`

Three sides and no angle means the cosine rule, with `\angle A O B` opposite $A B$

`(\sqrt{52})^{2} = (\sqrt{41})^{2} + (\sqrt{65})^{2} - 2 \times \sqrt{41} \times \sqrt{65} \times \text{cos} \angle A O B`

**[M1]**

Rearrange for the cosine, and note the squares simply undo the square roots

`\text{cos} \angle A O B = \frac{41 + 65 - 52}{2 \times \sqrt{41} \times \sqrt{65}}`

`\angle A O B = 58.465 \ldots ^{\circ}`

Now use the area formula with the two sides that enclose this angle

$\text{Area} = \frac{1}{2} \times \sqrt{41} \times \sqrt{65} \times \text{sin} 58 . 465 \dots ^{\circ}$

**[M1]**

$\text{Area} = 22$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: A correct expression, simplified or not, for `\left|\overset{\rightarrow}{O A}\right|` or `\left|\overset{\rightarrow}{O B}\right|`.
> 
> **M1**: A correct substitution into the cosine rule to find any angle of the triangle.
> 
> **M1**: A correct substitution into $\text{Area} = \frac{1}{2} a b \text{sin} C$, using your own lengths and angle.
> 
> **A1**: Accept answers which round to 22.
> 
> Any of the three angles may be used, provided the two sides in the area formula are the two that enclose it. Using `\angle O A B = 72.349 \ldots ^{\circ}` with $\sqrt{41}$ and $\sqrt{52}$, or `\angle A B O = 49.184 \ldots ^{\circ}` with $\sqrt{65}$ and $\sqrt{52}$, both reach the same area.
> 
> The determinant method is equally acceptable, and is marked like this. A correct statement of the area as $\frac{1}{2}$ times the determinant, listing the points in order and repeating the first at the end, earns the first mark. A correct evaluation of the determinant, ignoring the $\frac{1}{2}$, earns the second, and multiplying by $\frac{1}{2}$ earns the third, which a correct answer implies. The accuracy mark then requires the exact value 22 rather than a rounded one.
> 
> Heron's formula is also equally acceptable, and is marked like this. A correct length for `\left|\overset{\rightarrow}{O A}\right|` or `\left|\overset{\rightarrow}{O B}\right|` earns the first mark, finding half the perimeter earns the second, substituting into a correct Heron's formula earns the third, and the exact value 22 earns the fourth.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Vectors and trigonometry meet here, and the trigonometry is ordinary triangle work.
> 
> - Once you have the three side lengths, the vectors have done their job
> - Three sides and no angle is the standard cosine rule situation, exactly as in a non-vector question
> 
> Do not round the angle before using it.
> 
> - $58 . 465 \dots ^{\circ}$ carried in full gives exactly 22, while $58 . 5 ^{\circ}$ gives $22 . 01$
> - The area here is a whole number, which is a strong hint that no rounding should have crept in
> 
> The squares and square roots cancel in the cosine rule, so the arithmetic is tidier than it looks.
> 
> - $(\sqrt{41})^{2}=41$, so the numerator is just $41 + 65 - 52$
> - Leave the lengths as surds rather than converting them to decimals first
> 
> There is a much shorter route worth knowing.
> 
> - With $a$ and $b$ as perpendicular unit vectors, $\overset{\rightarrow}{OA}$ and $\overset{\rightarrow}{OB}$ behave like coordinates
> - The area is then `\frac{1}{2} \left|4 \times (- 1) - 8 \times 5\right|`, which gives 22 exactly in one line

parts.problemMd:
![Irregular triangle OAB with line CD intersecting at C. Points O, A, B form angles. Note: Diagram not accurately drawn. Caption states "Figure 2".](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-further-maths-19/geometry-and-trigonometry/trigonometric-formulae-and-identities/assets/007-irregular-triangle-oab-with-line-cd-intersecting.png)

Figure 2 shows triangle $AOB$

$\overset{\rightarrow}{OA}=4a+5b\overset{\rightarrow}{OB}=8a-b\overset{\rightarrow}{OD}=15a+10b$      where $\left|\mathbf{a}\right| = \left|\mathbf{b}\right| = 1$

The point $C$ lies on $AB$ and $OD$ such that $O$, $C$ and $D$ are collinear.

Use a vector method to find vector  $\overset{\rightarrow}{OC}$ as a simplified expression in terms of  $a$ and $b$
parts.solutionMd:
$C$ lies on two different lines, so write $\overset{\rightarrow}{OC}$ in two different ways and make them agree

$O$, $C$ and $D$ are collinear, so $\overset{\rightarrow}{OC}$ is a multiple of $\overset{\rightarrow}{OD}$

$\overset{\rightarrow}{OC} = λ ( 15 a + 10 b )$

**[M1]**

$C$ also lies on $A B$, so reach it by going out to $A$ and then part of the way along $\overset{\rightarrow}{AB}$

Part (a) gives $\overset{\rightarrow}{AB} = 4 a - 6 b$

$\overset{\rightarrow}{OC} = 4 a + 5 b + μ ( 4 a - 6 b )$

Collect the $a$ terms and the $b$ terms

$\overset{\rightarrow}{OC} = ( 4 + 4 μ ) a + ( 5 - 6 μ ) b$

**[M1]**

$a$ and $b$ point in different directions, so the only way two expressions can be equal is for the $a$ parts to match and the $b$ parts to match

$4 + 4 μ = 15 λ$

$5 - 6 μ = 10 λ$

Eliminate $λ$ by multiplying the first equation by 2 and the second by 3, making both right-hand sides $30 λ$

$8 + 8 μ = 15 - 18 μ$

**[M1]**

$26 μ = 7$

$μ = \frac{7}{26}$

**[A1]**

Substitute back into the expression for $\overset{\rightarrow}{OC}$ along $A B$

`\overset{\rightarrow}{O C} = \left(4 + 4 \times \frac{7}{26}\right) \mathbf{a} + \left(5 - 6 \times \frac{7}{26}\right) \mathbf{b}`

$\overset{\rightarrow}{OC} = \frac{66}{13} a + \frac{44}{13} b$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Writes $\overset{\rightarrow}{OC} = λ \overset{\rightarrow}{OD}$, or the equivalent with any letter.
> 
> **M1**: Writes $\overset{\rightarrow}{OC} = \overset{\rightarrow}{OA} + μ \overset{\rightarrow}{AB}$ and collects it into the form $( 4 + 4 μ ) a + ( 5 - 6 μ ) b$.
> 
> **M1**: Compares the $a$ and $b$ components to form two equations and solves them simultaneously. This mark depends on both earlier method marks.
> 
> **A1**: $μ = \frac{7}{26}$, or $λ = \frac{22}{65}$.
> 
> **A1**: $\overset{\rightarrow}{OC} = \frac{66}{13} a + \frac{44}{13} b$, or equivalently $5 \frac{1}{13} a + 3 \frac{5}{13} b$. The answer must be fully correct.
> 
> Substituting $λ = \frac{22}{65}$ into $λ ( 15 a + 10 b )$ reaches the same vector and is equally acceptable.
> 
> Going the other way round the triangle, $\overset{\rightarrow}{OC} = \overset{\rightarrow}{OB} + μ \overset{\rightarrow}{BA}$, is also equally acceptable.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Two routes to the same point is the standard method for an intersection.
> 
> - Being on $O D$ gives you one expression, being on $A B$ gives you another, and setting them equal is what pins the point down
> - Use two different letters for the two unknown multiples, or the algebra will collapse
> 
> Comparing components only works because $a$ and $b$ are independent.
> 
> - They point in different directions, so no amount of $a$ can ever make up a shortfall in $b$
> - That is what turns one vector equation into two ordinary simultaneous equations
> 
> Be careful about where the parameter starts from.
> 
> - $\overset{\rightarrow}{OC} = \overset{\rightarrow}{OA} + μ \overset{\rightarrow}{AB}$ means $μ$ measures the fraction of the way from $A$ to $B$
> - Writing $μ \overset{\rightarrow}{OB}$ by mistake is the commonest error, and it describes a completely different point
> 
> Do not stop at the value of the parameter.
> 
> - The question asks for $\overset{\rightarrow}{OC}$, so $μ = \frac{7}{26}$ is a stepping stone rather than the answer
> - Substituting back is worth a mark on its own, and the fractions do simplify neatly to thirteenths

parts.problemMd:
Using a [formula](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2026/02/33569-EDX%20IGCSE%20Further%20Pure%20Maths%20Formulae%20Sheet.pdf), show that

$\mathrm{cos}2θ=2\mathrm{cos}^{2}θ-1$
parts.solutionMd:
A double angle is an angle added to itself, so start from the addition formula on the formulae sheet

Use $\text{cos} ( A + B ) = \text{cos} A \text{cos} B - \text{sin} A \text{sin} B$ with both angles equal to $θ$

$\text{cos} 2 θ = \text{cos}^{2} θ - \text{sin}^{2} θ$

The target has only cosines in it, so replace the sine using $\text{sin}^{2} θ + \text{cos}^{2} θ \equiv 1$

$\text{cos} 2 θ = \text{cos}^{2} θ - ( 1 - \text{cos}^{2} θ )$

**[M1]**

Remove the bracket and collect the two cosine terms

$\text{cos} 2 θ = 2 \text{cos}^{2} θ - 1  \text{as required}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Expands $\text{cos} ( θ + θ )$ to $\text{cos}^{2} θ - \text{sin}^{2} θ$ and replaces $\text{sin}^{2} θ$ by $1 - \text{cos}^{2} θ$.
> 
> **A1**: Reaches the given result with no errors.
> 
> The answer is given, so the working must be complete.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The formulae sheet gives the addition formulae, and setting the two angles equal produces the double angle ones.
> 
> - $\text{cos} 2 θ = \text{cos} ( θ + θ )$ is the whole idea
> - The expansion $\text{cos}^{2} θ - \text{sin}^{2} θ$ is correct but is not the form asked for
> 
> Take care with the minus sign in front of the bracket.
> 
> - $\text{cos}^{2} θ - ( 1 - \text{cos}^{2} θ )$ gives $2 \text{cos}^{2} θ - 1$
> - Writing the substitution inside brackets and removing them on a separate line is what keeps the sign right
> 
> This one line is what makes the whole question work.
> 
> - $2 \text{cos}^{2} θ - 1$ cannot be integrated as it stands, but $\text{cos} 2 θ$ can
> - Parts (b) and (c) both depend on making that swap first

parts.problemMd:
Using a [formula](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2026/02/33569-EDX%20IGCSE%20Further%20Pure%20Maths%20Formulae%20Sheet.pdf), show that

$\mathrm{cos}2θ=2\mathrm{cos}^{2}θ-1$

Hence show that

$\int_{\frac{\pi}{3}}^{\frac{3 \pi}{4}} \left(2  cos^{2 } \theta - 1\right) d \theta = - \frac{a + \sqrt{b}}{c}$

where $a$, $b$ and $c$ are integers to be found.
parts.solutionMd:
$2 \text{cos}^{2} θ - 1$ cannot be integrated as it stands, but part (a) says it is exactly $\text{cos} 2 θ$, which can

Call the integral $I$ and make that swap first

`I = \int_{\frac{\pi}{3}}^{\frac{3 \pi}{4}} \text{cos} 2 \theta \text{d} \theta`

**[M1]**

Integrating $\text{cos} 2 θ$ gives $\frac{\text{sin}2θ}{2}$, dividing by the 2 inside the function

`I = \left[\frac{\text{sin} 2 \theta}{2}\right]_{\frac{\pi}{3}}^{\frac{3 \pi}{4}}`

**[M1]**

Substitute the limits, doubling each one before taking the sine

$I = \frac{\text{sin}\frac{3π}{2}}{2} - \frac{\text{sin}\frac{2π}{3}}{2}$

**[M1]**

$\text{sin} \frac{3π}{2} = - 1$ and $\text{sin} \frac{2π}{3} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$, both exact values

$I = - \frac{1}{2} - \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}$

Put both terms over 4 and take out the minus sign

$I = - \frac{2+\sqrt{3}}{4}$

**[A1]**

so $a = 2$, $b = 3$ and $c = 4$

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Replaces $2 \text{cos}^{2} θ - 1$ by $\text{cos} 2 θ$.
> 
> **M1**: Integrates to $\pm \frac{\text{sin}2θ}{2}$.
> 
> **M1**: Substitutes both limits correctly and subtracts.
> 
> **A1**: $- \frac{2+\sqrt{3}}{4}$, with the three values identified.
> 
> The answer is given in the question in the form $- \frac{a+\sqrt{b}}{c}$, so the working has to be complete.
> 
> Any equivalent correct set of values is accepted, so $a = 4$, $b = 12$, $c = 8$ would also be credited.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Part (a) is not decoration, it is the first line of part (b).
> 
> - A squared trigonometric function has no direct integral, so the double angle form is the only way in
> - Whenever a question proves an identity and then asks you to integrate, expect to use it immediately
> 
> Double the limits, not the answer.
> 
> - $\text{sin} 2 θ$ at $θ = \frac{3π}{4}$ means $\text{sin} \frac{3π}{2}$, not $\text{sin} \frac{3π}{4}$
> - Writing the doubled angle out before evaluating it is the habit that prevents this
> 
> A negative answer is expected here, so do not "correct" it.
> 
> - Between $\frac{π}{3}$ and $\frac{3π}{4}$ the curve $y = \text{cos} 2 θ$ lies below the axis
> - The question even prints a minus sign in the required form, which is a useful confirmation
> 
> Match your answer to the form asked for.
> 
> - The target is $- \frac{a+\sqrt{b}}{c}$ with integers, so $- \frac{1}{2} - \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}$ has to be combined over a single denominator
> - Stopping one line early is the commonest way to lose the accuracy mark on a question like this

parts.problemMd:
![Graph with two curves, \(C_1\) and \(C_2\), intersecting x-axis at O. Shaded region R between points A and B on horizontal axis \(θ\).
