Find $\overset{\rightarrow}{MA}$ as a simplified expression in terms of $p$ and $q$
parts.solutionMd:
$M$ is the midpoint of $O C$, so $\overset{\rightarrow}{OM}$ is half of $\overset{\rightarrow}{OC}$

`\overset{\rightarrow}{O M} = \frac{1}{2} \left(2 \mathbf{p} - 4 \mathbf{q}\right)`

$\overset{\rightarrow}{OM} = p - 2 q$

**[B1]**

There is no direct route from $M$ to $A$ in the information given, so travel back to $O$ and then out to $A$

$\overset{\rightarrow}{MA} = \overset{\rightarrow}{MO} + \overset{\rightarrow}{OA}$

Reversing a vector reverses its sign, so `\overset{\rightarrow}{M O} = - \left(\mathbf{p} - 2 \mathbf{q}\right)`

`\overset{\rightarrow}{M A} = - \left(\mathbf{p} - 2 \mathbf{q}\right) + 4 \mathbf{p} + 5 \mathbf{q}`

**[M1]**

Collect the $p$ terms and the $q$ terms separately

$\overset{\rightarrow}{MA} = 3 p + 7 q$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Either $\overset{\rightarrow}{OM} = p - 2 q$ or $\overset{\rightarrow}{MO} = - p + 2 q$. This may be embedded in your working for $\overset{\rightarrow}{MA}$ rather than written out on its own.
> 
> **M1**: A correct vector statement, so $\overset{\rightarrow}{MA} = \overset{\rightarrow}{MO} + \overset{\rightarrow}{OA}$, or $\overset{\rightarrow}{MA} = - \frac{1}{2} \overset{\rightarrow}{OC} + \overset{\rightarrow}{OA}$.
> 
> **A1**: The correct simplified vector, $\overset{\rightarrow}{MA} = 3 p + 7 q$.
> 
> $\overset{\rightarrow}{OB}$ is not needed in this part. It is given for part (b).

> **[exam-tip]**
> Halve the whole vector, not just one of its terms.
> 
> - `\frac{1}{2} \left(2 \mathbf{p} - 4 \mathbf{q}\right) = \mathbf{p} - 2 \mathbf{q}`, so both coefficients halve
> - Midpoint questions are where a dropped factor of $\frac{1}{2}$ costs the whole of a later part
> 
> Build the vector by walking a path through a point you know.
> 
> - $\overset{\rightarrow}{MA} = \overset{\rightarrow}{MO} + \overset{\rightarrow}{OA}$ works because the middle letters match up and cancel
> - Everything in this question is measured from $O$, so every path goes back through $O$
> 
> Reverse the whole bracket, signs included.
> 
> - $\overset{\rightarrow}{MO}$ is $\overset{\rightarrow}{OM}$ with every sign changed, so `- \left(\mathbf{p} - 2 \mathbf{q}\right)` becomes $- p + 2 q$
> - The $q$ term turns positive here, which is what makes the answer $7 q$ rather than $3 q$

parts.problemMd:
The point $N$ lies on $OB$ such that $M$,  $N$ and $A$are collinear.

Find the ratio $MN:NA$
parts.solutionMd:
$N$ lies on two different lines, so write $\overset{\rightarrow}{MN}$ in two different ways and make them agree

$M$, $N$ and $A$ are collinear, so $\overset{\rightarrow}{MN}$ is a multiple of $\overset{\rightarrow}{MA}$ from part (a)

`\overset{\rightarrow}{M N} = \lambda \left(3 \mathbf{p} + 7 \mathbf{q}\right)`

**[M1]**

$N$ also lies on $O B$, so reach it from $M$ by going back to $O$ and then part of the way along $\overset{\rightarrow}{OB}$

$\overset{\rightarrow}{MN} = \overset{\rightarrow}{MO} + μ \overset{\rightarrow}{OB}$

`\overset{\rightarrow}{M N} = - \left(\mathbf{p} - 2 \mathbf{q}\right) + \mu \left(3 \mathbf{p} + \mathbf{q}\right)`

Collect the $p$ terms and the $q$ terms

`\overset{\rightarrow}{M N} = \left(- 1 + 3 \mu\right) \mathbf{p} + \left(2 + \mu\right) \mathbf{q}`

**[M1]**

$p$ and $q$ point in different directions, so the $p$ parts must match and the $q$ parts must match

$3 λ = - 1 + 3 μ$

$7 λ = 2 + μ$

**[M1]**

Rearrange the second equation for $μ$ and substitute it into the first

$μ = 7 λ - 2$

`3 \lambda = - 1 + 3 \left(7 \lambda - 2\right)`

$3 λ = 21 λ - 7$

**[M1]**

$18 λ = 7$

$λ = \frac{7}{18}$

**[A1]**

$λ$ is the fraction of $\overset{\rightarrow}{MA}$ covered by $\overset{\rightarrow}{MN}$, so $M N$ is 7 parts out of 18 and $N A$ is the remaining 11

$M N : N A = 7 : 11$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: One vector expression for $\overset{\rightarrow}{MN}$ or $\overset{\rightarrow}{AN}$ involving a parameter. Any path may be used, provided it involves one of those two vectors.
> 
> **M1**: A second expression for $\overset{\rightarrow}{MN}$ or $\overset{\rightarrow}{AN}$ by a different path, involving a second, different parameter.
> 
> **M1**: Equates the $p$ and $q$ coefficients to form a pair of simultaneous equations, both of which must be in terms of the two parameters.
> 
> **M1**: An attempt to solve your simultaneous equations. Allow up to one processing error. This mark depends on the previous method mark.
> 
> **A1**: $λ = \frac{7}{18}$. The second parameter is not required, but its value is $μ = \frac{13}{18}$.
> 
> **A1**: $M N : N A = 7 : 11$.
> 
> The parameters need not be called $λ$ and $μ$, and the routes may be chosen freely as long as the two are genuinely different. Working with $\overset{\rightarrow}{AN}$ instead, so `\overset{\rightarrow}{A N} = k \left(- 3 \mathbf{p} - 7 \mathbf{q}\right)` together with $\overset{\rightarrow}{AN} = \overset{\rightarrow}{AO} + l \overset{\rightarrow}{OB}$, reaches the same ratio and earns the same marks.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Two expressions for the same point is the standard method whenever two lines cross.
> 
> - Lying on $M A$ gives you one expression, lying on $O B$ gives you another, and setting them equal is what pins $N$ down
> - Use two different letters for the two unknown multiples, or the two equations become one
> 
> Comparing components only works because $p$ and $q$ are independent.
> 
> - They point in different directions, so no amount of $p$ can ever make up a shortfall in $q$
> - That is what turns a single vector equation into two ordinary simultaneous equations
> 
> A fraction is not a ratio, so do not stop at $λ$.
> 
> - $λ = \frac{7}{18}$ says $M N$ is 7 of the 18 equal parts of $M A$, which leaves 11 parts for $N A$
> - The ratio is $7 : 11$, not $7 : 18$, and writing the wrong one loses the final mark
> 
> Sketching the quadrilateral pays for itself here.
> 
> - Marking $M$, $N$ and the three given vectors on a diagram makes the two routes to $N$ obvious
> - The official scheme prints its own sketch for exactly that reason, and it is reproduced below

parts.problemMd:
![Triangle OAB with lines AM and BN intersecting at X. Points M and N lie on sides OA and OB, respectively. 'Diagram NOT accurately drawn.'](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-further-maths-19/vectors/vectors/assets/001-triangle-oab-with-lines-am-and-bn-intersecting-a.png)

Figure 3 shows triangle $OAB$ with $\overset{\rightarrow}{OA}=a$ and $\overset{\rightarrow}{OB}=b$

$M$ is the midpoint of $OA$.

$N$ is the point on $OB$ such that $ON:NB=3:1$

The lines $AN$ and $BM$ intersect at the point $X$.

Find expressions, in terms of $a$and $b$, for

(i) $\overset{\rightarrow}{AN}$

[2]

(ii) $\overset{\rightarrow}{BM}$

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
**(i)**

$N$ divides $O B$ with $O N : N B = 3 : 1$, which makes four equal parts, so $\overset{\rightarrow}{ON}$ is three quarters of $\overset{\rightarrow}{OB}$

$\overset{\rightarrow}{ON} = \frac{3}{4} b$

There is no direct route from $A$ to $N$, so travel back to $O$ and then out to $N$

$\overset{\rightarrow}{AN} = \overset{\rightarrow}{AO} + \overset{\rightarrow}{ON}$

**[M1]**

$\overset{\rightarrow}{AO}$ is $\overset{\rightarrow}{OA}$ reversed, so it is $- a$

$\overset{\rightarrow}{AN} = - a + \frac{3}{4} b$

**[A1]**

**(ii)**

Do the same from $B$, going back to $O$ and then out to $M$

$M$ is the midpoint of $O A$, so $\overset{\rightarrow}{OM}$ is half of $a$

$\overset{\rightarrow}{BM} = \overset{\rightarrow}{BO} + \overset{\rightarrow}{OM}$

$\overset{\rightarrow}{BM} = - b + \frac{1}{2} a$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: A correct vector path for $\overset{\rightarrow}{AN}$, so $\overset{\rightarrow}{AO} + \overset{\rightarrow}{ON}$ or $\overset{\rightarrow}{AO} + \frac{3}{4} \overset{\rightarrow}{OB}$. A fully correct answer implies this mark.
> 
> **A1**: $\overset{\rightarrow}{AN} = - a + \frac{3}{4} b$.
> 
> **B1**: $\overset{\rightarrow}{BM} = - b + \frac{1}{2} a$.
> 
> Part (ii) carries a single mark for the answer, with no separate mark for the path, so an unsupported correct vector earns it in full.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Turn the ratio into a fraction of the whole line before you use it.
> 
> - $O N : N B = 3 : 1$ makes $3 + 1 = 4$ equal parts, so $\overset{\rightarrow}{ON} = \frac{3}{4} b$
> - Writing $\frac{3}{1}$ or $\frac{1}{3}$ instead is the commonest slip, and it wrecks part (b) as well as this one
> 
> Both vectors are built the same way, so set them out the same way.
> 
> - $\overset{\rightarrow}{AN} = \overset{\rightarrow}{AO} + \overset{\rightarrow}{ON}$ and $\overset{\rightarrow}{BM} = \overset{\rightarrow}{BO} + \overset{\rightarrow}{OM}$ are the same idea with the letters swapped
> - Every vector here is measured from $O$, so every path starts by going back to $O$
> 
> Leave your answers exactly as you find them.
> 
> - $- a + \frac{3}{4} b$ and $- b + \frac{1}{2} a$ are what part (b) needs, so there is nothing to tidy up
> - Both will be multiplied by an unknown in a moment, so keeping the fractions is easier than clearing them

parts.problemMd: Using a vector method, find $AX:XN$
parts.solutionMd:
$X$ lies on both $A N$ and $B M$, so write $\overset{\rightarrow}{AX}$ in two different ways and make them agree

$X$ is on $A N$, so $\overset{\rightarrow}{AX}$ is a multiple of $\overset{\rightarrow}{AN}$ from part (a)

`\overset{\rightarrow}{A X} = \lambda \left(- \mathbf{a} + \frac{3}{4} \mathbf{b}\right)`

**[B1]**

$X$ is also on $B M$, so reach it from $A$ by going to $M$ and then part of the way along $\overset{\rightarrow}{MB}$

$M$ is the midpoint of $O A$, so going from $A$ to $M$ means travelling half of $a$ backwards

$\overset{\rightarrow}{AM} = - \frac{1}{2} a$

$\overset{\rightarrow}{MB}$ is part (a)'s $\overset{\rightarrow}{BM}$ reversed

$\overset{\rightarrow}{MB} = - \frac{1}{2} a + b$

`\overset{\rightarrow}{A X} = - \frac{1}{2} \mathbf{a} + \mu \left(- \frac{1}{2} \mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b}\right)`

**[M1]**

$a$ and $b$ point in different directions, so the $a$ parts of the two expressions must match, and so must the $b$ parts

$- λ = - \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{2} μ$

**[M1]**

$\frac{3}{4} λ = μ$

**[M1]**

Substitute the second equation into the first, so that only $λ$ is left

$- λ = - \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{3}{4} λ$

$- λ + \frac{3}{8} λ = - \frac{1}{2}$

$- \frac{5}{8} λ = - \frac{1}{2}$

**[M1]**

$λ = \frac{4}{5}$

**[A1]**

$λ$ is the fraction of $\overset{\rightarrow}{AN}$ covered by $\overset{\rightarrow}{AX}$, so $A X$ is 4 parts out of 5 and $X N$ is the remaining 1

$A X : X N = 4 : 1$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: A valid vector for $\overset{\rightarrow}{AX}$ carrying a parameter, so `\lambda \left(- \mathbf{a} + \frac{3}{4} \mathbf{b}\right)`, using your part (a) answer. Allow follow-through, allow the reverse direction, and allow it to be embedded in your working.
> 
> **M1**: A second valid path for $\overset{\rightarrow}{AX}$ with a second, different parameter, so $\overset{\rightarrow}{AM} + μ \overset{\rightarrow}{MB}$. It must be a genuinely different route, not a second journey along the same line.
> 
> **M1**: Correctly equates the $a$ components of your two expressions.
> 
> **M1**: Correctly equates the $b$ components of your two expressions.
> 
> **M1**: An attempt to solve your simultaneous equations. There may be errors, but it must be clear that you are solving them to reach a value for one of your parameters. This mark depends on both earlier method marks.
> 
> **A1**: A correct value for one of your parameters, so $λ = \frac{4}{5}$ with $μ = \frac{3}{5}$.
> 
> **A1**: $A X : X N = 4 : 1$.
> 
> The parameters need not be called $λ$ and $μ$, and their signs depend on the direction each route is taken in. Setting the routes up with one or both vectors reversed gives $λ = - \frac{4}{5}$ with $μ = \frac{3}{5}$, or $λ = \frac{4}{5}$ with $μ = - \frac{3}{5}$, or $λ = - \frac{4}{5}$ with $μ = - \frac{3}{5}$, and each is correct for the route that produced it.
> 
> Reaching $X$ the long way round, $\overset{\rightarrow}{AX} = \overset{\rightarrow}{AB} + \overset{\rightarrow}{BN} + λ \overset{\rightarrow}{AN}$, is equally acceptable and gives $λ = \frac{1}{5}$ with $μ = \frac{3}{5}$, reaching the same ratio.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Two expressions for the same point is the standard method whenever two lines cross.
> 
> - Lying on $A N$ gives you one expression, lying on $B M$ gives you another, and setting them equal is what pins $X$ down
> - The two routes must be genuinely different, so travelling along $A N$ twice gets you nowhere
> 
> Watch the direction of the short hop to $M$.
> 
> - $M$ is the midpoint of $O A$, so going from $A$ to $M$ moves you back towards $O$ and $\overset{\rightarrow}{AM} = - \frac{1}{2} a$
> - Writing $+ \frac{1}{2} a$ here puts $X$ on the wrong side of $A$ entirely
> 
> Equating the two components gives you two separate marks.
> 
> - One mark is for the $a$ equation and one for the $b$ equation, so write both out even if you can see the answer
> - Each equation is worth as much as the algebra that follows it
> 
> Convert the fraction into the ratio at the end.
> 
> - $λ = \frac{4}{5}$ means $A X$ is 4 of the 5 equal parts of $A N$, leaving 1 part for $X N$
> - The answer is $4 : 1$, not $4 : 5$, and that last step carries its own mark
